title: Introduction: Formulation of the problem

paragraphs.text: 1 1 Introduction: Formulation of the Problem
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The heart is the youngest, most diverse, most fluid, most changeable, most versatile part of creation.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Goethe1
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Congenital heart disease (con, together; genitus, born) is often looked upon as a group of gross structural abnormalities that are present at birth. While not incorrect, this definition requires elaboration and qualification.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Prenatal diagnoses have been possible for over 30 years.2 Beginning about embryonic day 20 in the human fetus, progenitor cells within the mesoderm become committed to a cardiogenic destination.3 The majority of malformations compatible with 6 months of intrauterine life permit live offspring at term. A given malformation may exist in relative harmony with the fetal circulation, only to be modified considerably, at least physiologically, by dramatic circulatory changes at birth.4 Weeks, months, or years may then elapse before an anomaly reveals itself as characteristic or typical. A functionally normal aortic valve that is congenitally bicuspid at birth may take decades to fibrose, calcify, and present as overt aortic stenosis. Conversely, a malformation may disappear, as is the case with spontaneous closure of a ventricular septal defect.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Congenital malformations of the heart and circulation are not fixed anatomic defects that appear at birth, but instead are anomalies in flux that originate in the early embryo, evolve during gestation, survive the dramatic circulatory alterations at birth, and change considerably during the course of extrauterine life. Congenital heart disease was once the exclusive and legitimate domain of pediatrics, but survival patterns have changed appreciably.5 In the United States today, two-thirds of the congenital heart disease population are adults,6,7 creating a new generation of patients who are best cared for by specially trained cardiologists.8
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Furthermore, certain defects that are actually or potentially of functional significance are not gross structurally, such as congenital complete heart block, either isolated (see Chapter 4) or with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (see Chapter 6), or with left isomerism (see Chapter 3); Wolff- Parkinson-White preexcitation, either isolated or complicated (see Chapter 13); absence of a sinus node as with a superior vena caval sinus venosus atrial septal defect (see Chapter 15) or left isomerism (see Chapter 3); ventricular tachycardia with the long QT syndromes,9 or arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia (see Chapter 13). Still other abnormalities, such as Marfan syndrome, which is the result of mutations in the gene that encodes fibrillin-1, are actually or potentially of functional significance, but they do not necessarily manifest at birth as gross structural malformations and, as a matter of convention, are usually not classified as congenital.10 There are also anomalies that may escape inclusion as defects, such as congenital kinking of the internal carotid artery.11
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Because of the intimate interplay between congenital malformations of the heart and the fetal substrate, let us now turn to the fetal circulation per se, and the remarkable circulatory changes that occur at birth.4,12,13 In utero patterns of blood flow have been defined in fetal lambs after inserting catheters into limb vessels,4 and in utero left and right ventricular outputs and flow distributions through the foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, and pulmonary bed have been measured in human fetuses with
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: high-resolution color Doppler ultrasonography.12,14 The right and left ventricles do not function in series in the fetus as they do in the extrauterine circulation. Gas exchange occurs in the placenta, not in the lungs. About two-thirds of the right ventricular output is diverted away from the lungs through a wide patent ductus arteriosus into the descending thoracic aorta, from which a large portion enters the umbilical circulation for oxygenation in the placenta. Pulmonary blood flow is low but meets nutritional requirements for growth of the lungs. Inferior vena cava blood, which is a composite from the umbilical vein, the left and right hepatic veins, the ductus venosus, and the distal inferior vena cava, streams in the direction of the foramen ovale into the left atrium and then into the left ventricle, assisted by the eustachian valve. About 60% of the umbilical venous return that is oxygenated in the placenta bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus and enters the inferior vena cava and right atrium. Blood from the superior vena cava is deflected within the right atrium toward the tricuspid valve, across which it reaches the right ventricle. About 70% of the relatively oxygen-rich blood ejected from the left ventricle is distributed to the coronary circulation (and thus the myocardium), to the head and neck (and thus the brain), and to the forelimbs. Almost 90% of the relatively oxygen-poor blood ejected by the right ventricle passes through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta to be oxygenated in the placenta. Accordingly, the fetal circulation is designed so that blood with higher oxygen saturation preferentially reaches the myocardium and brain, and less saturated blood preferentially reaches the placenta.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The profound circulatory changes at birth occur almost simultaneously. The umbilical/placental circulation is eliminated, the lungs expand, rhythmic ventilation commences, oxygen tension rises as alveolar fluid is eliminated and ambient air is breathed, pulmonary vascular resistance falls, and pulmonary blood flow increases eight- to ten-fold. Venous return to the left atrium increases, left atrial pressure rises, the valve of the foramen ovale closes, and the ductus arteriosus functionally closes (constricts) within hours after birth, effectively separating the pulmonary and systemic circulations.4 These changes have significant impact on infants born with congenital heart disease where a circulation in series may fail to be established in the presence of intracardiac shunting.13 Other important changes relate to the fetal right ventricle, which slowly loses its relative mass. With the stimulus of afterload eliminated, there is a gradual reduction in right ventricular wall thickness relative to the ventricular septum and left ventricle. The neonatal right ventricle does not undergo regression, but instead does not increase its mass as rapidly as the left ventricle. Normal physiologic adaptations at birth are remarkable in their own right. It is therefore not surprising that congenital malformations of the heart or circulation will, to varying degrees, interact with and be modified by extrauterine life.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: “One of the most wondrous features of animate nature must surely be the perfect harmony existing between structure and function.”14 No organ system exemplifies this as well as the heart and circulation. In the presence of congenital heart disease, both the morphology
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: and physiology of the heart and circulation change with the passage of time from the fetus, to the neonate, to the infant, to the child, to the adolescent, and to the adult. Some of these changes result in neonatal death, while others express themselves gradually over weeks, months, years, or even decades. The clinical manifestations of congenital heart disease are dealt with herein in terms of anatomic and physiologic mechanisms. The method of assessment employed in the process of clinical recognition is a syllogism of applied logic. When conclusions are drawn from accurate observations, correct diagnoses emerge with gratifying frequency, even when the malformations are complex. Logic is encouraged; memorization is minimized. In each chapter, the gross morphology is first established in order to shed light on the physiologic derangements. The question is then asked: What clinical manifestations might result from these anatomic and physiologic derangements? The stage is now set for clinical recognition—the thesis of this book—which depends on a synthesis of information from the history, the physical examination, the electrocardiogram, the chest x-ray, and more advanced imaging, such as with cardiac computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Contemporary imaging techniques serve as important supplements.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The history, which is an interview, is designed to secure background information. The physical examination includes the physical appearance, the arterial pulse, the jugular venous pulse, precordial percussion, movement and palpation, and auscultation.15 The stethoscope is the oldest cardiovascular diagnostic instrument in continuous clinical use. The electrocardiogram, developed in 1903 by Willem Einthoven, when read closely and interpreted in clinical context, provides gratifying diagnostic insights, even in complex congenital heart disease.16 Meticulous attention should be devoted to the P wave, the P duration, the PR interval, the QRS, the QT interval, and the T wave. The electrocardiographic waves are believed to have been so-named by Rene Descartes, an 18th century French philosopher and scientist17 who was surely known to Einthoven. The x-ray was developed in 1895 by Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen. Chest x-rays must be read closely and interpreted in clinical context. Posteroanterior and lateral views should be read according to a planned sequence, namely penetration, rotation, degree of inhalation, age and sex, right/left orientation, thoracic and abdominal situs, positions and malpositions above and below the diaphragm, the bones, the extrapulmonary soft tissue densities, the vascular and parenchymal intrapulmonary soft tissue densities, the great arteries and great veins, the atria, and the ventricles. There is much to be said for learning interpretation by reading chest x-rays with a trained chest radiologist. As with the electrocardiogram, the amount of information that can be extracted from chest x-rays is gratifying, even in complex congenital heart disease.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: It is axiomatic that emphasis should be placed on the relationship of the parts to the whole, a relationship that results in a harmonious picture devoid of contradictions, rather than a collection of loosely related observations. Maximum information should be extracted from each source while relating information from one source to that of another. Each step should advance our thinking and narrow the diagnostic possibilities. By the end of the clinical assessment, untenable considerations should have been discarded, possibilities retained for further consideration, and probabilities brought into sharper focus. The process reflects Herophilus’ adage that the best physician is one who distinguishes between the possible and the impossible.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: A diagnostic impression, once entertained, necessarily influences the objectivity with which subsequent impressions are appraised. If the same sequence of clinical evaluation is always employed, the later steps cannot be objectively assessed. It is therefore useful to vary the sequence with which information is assembled. Begin, for example, with the chest x-ray or electrocardiogram. With infants, it is often practical to take advantage of
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: temporary periods of calm and start with the physical examination, which may shortly be difficult to perform. It is not the sequence that matters, but the depth and synthesis of analysis. Irrespective of how the order of information is arranged, two questions must always be asked: how does one step relate to the next, and how do the parts relate to the whole?
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Diagnostic thinking benefits from employing anticipation and supposition. After drawing conclusions from the history, it is useful to pause and ask: if these assumptions are correct, what can be anticipated from the physical examination, or what specific points can be anticipated in the electrocardiogram or x-ray to support or refute initial impressions? Anticipation heightens interest as the clinical assessment progresses. Confirmation comes as a source of satisfaction, and error stands out in bold relief. Nor should we be afraid of mistakes. Truth emerges sooner from error than from confusion.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of congenital heart disease can be complex,18 particularly in adults, but a thoughtful systematic approach can be helpful. Decades ago, Paul Wood proposed that we answer five clinical cornerstone questions in understanding the derangements of the heart and circulation seen across lesions (Box 1.1). When approached according to this proposal, the clinical recognition of congenital heart disease becomes a stimulating challenge, a satisfying discipline in logical thinking, and a constant source of self-education. The intensity of inquiry and the analytical standards employed at the bedside should be the same as those in diagnostic laboratories. Fig. 1.1 offers an approach to diagnosis based on the simple observation of the presence or absence of cyanosis, and the presence or absence of a scar on the chest, its location, and the date at which the patient underwent the associated procedure. Table 1.1 summarizes the key findings in some of the most common congenital lesions.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: In the Preface to the first edition of Clinical Recognition of Congenital Heart Disease, Dr. Perloff said, “I hope to stimulate clinicians to use the basic tools readily at their disposal—the history, the physical examination, the electrocardiogram, and the chest x-ray.” The Preface to the third edition stated that, “Two-dimensional echocardiography was in its infancy when the second edition appeared, but now is a routine laboratory procedure.” Cardiac catheterization and angiography were followed by transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography, and MRI, magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), and CT now provide exquisite anatomic detail and refined physiologic information.19–25
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Given these advanced imaging techniques, and with more in the offing, has emphasis on the history, physical examination, electrocardiogram, chest x-ray, and echocardiogram become irrelevant? Intelligent selection of investigative procedures from an ever-increasing array requires far more sophisticated decisionmaking than was necessary when choices were limited to the electrocardiogram and chest x-ray. The basic clinical assessment provides the information necessary for most of these decisions. With increasing emphasis on the cost of medical care, it is likely that there will be a resurgence of interest in the inexpensive and safe clinical examination.26
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Some additional points: The term natural history is not used. Julien Hoffman’s definition is relevant: “The natural history of any disease is a description of what happens to people with the disease who do not receive treatment for it.”27 Natural history is therefore not synonymous with unoperated, and unnatural history is not synonymous with postoperative. Nonsurgical therapeutic interventions can hardly be considered natural. A second point: differential diagnoses are not employed. Instead, each chapter ends with a summary that permits clinical recognition of the congenital anomaly covered in the chapter. These summaries bring together clinical highlights and serve as reminders for the reader’s convenience.
paragraphs.heading: BOX 1.1 Five Basic Questions

paragraphs.text: support for the development of a unified system for describing congenial cardiac malformations.28 The terms used herein to describe congenital malformations of the heart and circulation include older latinized forms and more recent anglicized forms.29–31 The vocabulary of congenital heart disease is replete with abbreviations understood only by the initiated. Accordingly, when abbreviations are used, they will first be defined for the reader’s convenience, but full terms will subsequently be used. New terms are not employed when old terms suffice. Acronyms are avoided.

The terminology was assiduously addressed, and based on decades of personal experience, Dr. Perloff’s objective, so carefully transmitted to us, remains to excite interest and to be clearly understood.

# 1. Introduction: Formulation of the problem
> [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md).


## PDF page 15 | printed page 1

1 1 Introduction: Formulation of the Problem

The heart is the youngest, most diverse, most fluid, most changeable, most versatile part of creation.

Goethe1

Congenital heart disease (con, together; genitus, born) is often looked upon as a group of gross structural abnormalities that are present at birth. While not incorrect, this definition requires elaboration and qualification.

Prenatal diagnoses have been possible for over 30 years.2 Beginning about embryonic day 20 in the human fetus, progenitor cells within the mesoderm become committed to a cardiogenic destination.3 The majority of malformations compatible with 6 months of intrauterine life permit live offspring at term. A given malformation may exist in relative harmony with the fetal circulation, only to be modified considerably, at least physiologically, by dramatic circulatory changes at birth.4 Weeks, months, or years may then elapse before an anomaly reveals itself as characteristic or typical. A functionally normal aortic valve that is congenitally bicuspid at birth may take decades to fibrose, calcify, and present as overt aortic stenosis. Conversely, a malformation may disappear, as is the case with spontaneous closure of a ventricular septal defect.

Congenital malformations of the heart and circulation are not fixed anatomic defects that appear at birth, but instead are anomalies in flux that originate in the early embryo, evolve during gestation, survive the dramatic circulatory alterations at birth, and change considerably during the course of extrauterine life. Congenital heart disease was once the exclusive and legitimate domain of pediatrics, but survival patterns have changed appreciably.5 In the United States today, two-thirds of the congenital heart disease population are adults,6,7 creating a new generation of patients who are best cared for by specially trained cardiologists.8

Furthermore, certain defects that are actually or potentially of functional significance are not gross structurally, such as congenital complete heart block, either isolated (see Chapter 4) or with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (see Chapter 6), or with left isomerism (see Chapter 3); Wolff- Parkinson-White preexcitation, either isolated or complicated (see Chapter 13); absence of a sinus node as with a superior vena caval sinus venosus atrial septal defect (see Chapter 15) or left isomerism (see Chapter 3); ventricular tachycardia with the long QT syndromes,9 or arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia (see Chapter 13). Still other abnormalities, such as Marfan syndrome, which is the result of mutations in the gene that encodes fibrillin-1, are actually or potentially of functional significance, but they do not necessarily manifest at birth as gross structural malformations and, as a matter of convention, are usually not classified as congenital.10 There are also anomalies that may escape inclusion as defects, such as congenital kinking of the internal carotid artery.11

Because of the intimate interplay between congenital malformations of the heart and the fetal substrate, let us now turn to the fetal circulation per se, and the remarkable circulatory changes that occur at birth.4,12,13 In utero patterns of blood flow have been defined in fetal lambs after inserting catheters into limb vessels,4 and in utero left and right ventricular outputs and flow distributions through the foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, and pulmonary bed have been measured in human fetuses with

high-resolution color Doppler ultrasonography.12,14 The right and left ventricles do not function in series in the fetus as they do in the extrauterine circulation. Gas exchange occurs in the placenta, not in the lungs. About two-thirds of the right ventricular output is diverted away from the lungs through a wide patent ductus arteriosus into the descending thoracic aorta, from which a large portion enters the umbilical circulation for oxygenation in the placenta. Pulmonary blood flow is low but meets nutritional requirements for growth of the lungs. Inferior vena cava blood, which is a composite from the umbilical vein, the left and right hepatic veins, the ductus venosus, and the distal inferior vena cava, streams in the direction of the foramen ovale into the left atrium and then into the left ventricle, assisted by the eustachian valve. About 60% of the umbilical venous return that is oxygenated in the placenta bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus and enters the inferior vena cava and right atrium. Blood from the superior vena cava is deflected within the right atrium toward the tricuspid valve, across which it reaches the right ventricle. About 70% of the relatively oxygen-rich blood ejected from the left ventricle is distributed to the coronary circulation (and thus the myocardium), to the head and neck (and thus the brain), and to the forelimbs. Almost 90% of the relatively oxygen-poor blood ejected by the right ventricle passes through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta to be oxygenated in the placenta. Accordingly, the fetal circulation is designed so that blood with higher oxygen saturation preferentially reaches the myocardium and brain, and less saturated blood preferentially reaches the placenta.

The profound circulatory changes at birth occur almost simultaneously. The umbilical/placental circulation is eliminated, the lungs expand, rhythmic ventilation commences, oxygen tension rises as alveolar fluid is eliminated and ambient air is breathed, pulmonary vascular resistance falls, and pulmonary blood flow increases eight- to ten-fold. Venous return to the left atrium increases, left atrial pressure rises, the valve of the foramen ovale closes, and the ductus arteriosus functionally closes (constricts) within hours after birth, effectively separating the pulmonary and systemic circulations.4 These changes have significant impact on infants born with congenital heart disease where a circulation in series may fail to be established in the presence of intracardiac shunting.13 Other important changes relate to the fetal right ventricle, which slowly loses its relative mass. With the stimulus of afterload eliminated, there is a gradual reduction in right ventricular wall thickness relative to the ventricular septum and left ventricle. The neonatal right ventricle does not undergo regression, but instead does not increase its mass as rapidly as the left ventricle. Normal physiologic adaptations at birth are remarkable in their own right. It is therefore not surprising that congenital malformations of the heart or circulation will, to varying degrees, interact with and be modified by extrauterine life.

“One of the most wondrous features of animate nature must surely be the perfect harmony existing between structure and function.”14 No organ system exemplifies this as well as the heart and circulation. In the presence of congenital heart disease, both the morphology


## PDF page 16 | printed page 2

and physiology of the heart and circulation change with the passage of time from the fetus, to the neonate, to the infant, to the child, to the adolescent, and to the adult. Some of these changes result in neonatal death, while others express themselves gradually over weeks, months, years, or even decades. The clinical manifestations of congenital heart disease are dealt with herein in terms of anatomic and physiologic mechanisms. The method of assessment employed in the process of clinical recognition is a syllogism of applied logic. When conclusions are drawn from accurate observations, correct diagnoses emerge with gratifying frequency, even when the malformations are complex. Logic is encouraged; memorization is minimized. In each chapter, the gross morphology is first established in order to shed light on the physiologic derangements. The question is then asked: What clinical manifestations might result from these anatomic and physiologic derangements? The stage is now set for clinical recognition—the thesis of this book—which depends on a synthesis of information from the history, the physical examination, the electrocardiogram, the chest x-ray, and more advanced imaging, such as with cardiac computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Contemporary imaging techniques serve as important supplements.

The history, which is an interview, is designed to secure background information. The physical examination includes the physical appearance, the arterial pulse, the jugular venous pulse, precordial percussion, movement and palpation, and auscultation.15 The stethoscope is the oldest cardiovascular diagnostic instrument in continuous clinical use. The electrocardiogram, developed in 1903 by Willem Einthoven, when read closely and interpreted in clinical context, provides gratifying diagnostic insights, even in complex congenital heart disease.16 Meticulous attention should be devoted to the P wave, the P duration, the PR interval, the QRS, the QT interval, and the T wave. The electrocardiographic waves are believed to have been so-named by Rene Descartes, an 18th century French philosopher and scientist17 who was surely known to Einthoven. The x-ray was developed in 1895 by Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen. Chest x-rays must be read closely and interpreted in clinical context. Posteroanterior and lateral views should be read according to a planned sequence, namely penetration, rotation, degree of inhalation, age and sex, right/left orientation, thoracic and abdominal situs, positions and malpositions above and below the diaphragm, the bones, the extrapulmonary soft tissue densities, the vascular and parenchymal intrapulmonary soft tissue densities, the great arteries and great veins, the atria, and the ventricles. There is much to be said for learning interpretation by reading chest x-rays with a trained chest radiologist. As with the electrocardiogram, the amount of information that can be extracted from chest x-rays is gratifying, even in complex congenital heart disease.

It is axiomatic that emphasis should be placed on the relationship of the parts to the whole, a relationship that results in a harmonious picture devoid of contradictions, rather than a collection of loosely related observations. Maximum information should be extracted from each source while relating information from one source to that of another. Each step should advance our thinking and narrow the diagnostic possibilities. By the end of the clinical assessment, untenable considerations should have been discarded, possibilities retained for further consideration, and probabilities brought into sharper focus. The process reflects Herophilus’ adage that the best physician is one who distinguishes between the possible and the impossible.

A diagnostic impression, once entertained, necessarily influences the objectivity with which subsequent impressions are appraised. If the same sequence of clinical evaluation is always employed, the later steps cannot be objectively assessed. It is therefore useful to vary the sequence with which information is assembled. Begin, for example, with the chest x-ray or electrocardiogram. With infants, it is often practical to take advantage of

temporary periods of calm and start with the physical examination, which may shortly be difficult to perform. It is not the sequence that matters, but the depth and synthesis of analysis. Irrespective of how the order of information is arranged, two questions must always be asked: how does one step relate to the next, and how do the parts relate to the whole?

Diagnostic thinking benefits from employing anticipation and supposition. After drawing conclusions from the history, it is useful to pause and ask: if these assumptions are correct, what can be anticipated from the physical examination, or what specific points can be anticipated in the electrocardiogram or x-ray to support or refute initial impressions? Anticipation heightens interest as the clinical assessment progresses. Confirmation comes as a source of satisfaction, and error stands out in bold relief. Nor should we be afraid of mistakes. Truth emerges sooner from error than from confusion.

The clinical presentation of congenital heart disease can be complex,18 particularly in adults, but a thoughtful systematic approach can be helpful. Decades ago, Paul Wood proposed that we answer five clinical cornerstone questions in understanding the derangements of the heart and circulation seen across lesions (Box 1.1). When approached according to this proposal, the clinical recognition of congenital heart disease becomes a stimulating challenge, a satisfying discipline in logical thinking, and a constant source of self-education. The intensity of inquiry and the analytical standards employed at the bedside should be the same as those in diagnostic laboratories. Fig. 1.1 offers an approach to diagnosis based on the simple observation of the presence or absence of cyanosis, and the presence or absence of a scar on the chest, its location, and the date at which the patient underwent the associated procedure. Table 1.1 summarizes the key findings in some of the most common congenital lesions.

In the Preface to the first edition of Clinical Recognition of Congenital Heart Disease, Dr. Perloff said, “I hope to stimulate clinicians to use the basic tools readily at their disposal—the history, the physical examination, the electrocardiogram, and the chest x-ray.” The Preface to the third edition stated that, “Two-dimensional echocardiography was in its infancy when the second edition appeared, but now is a routine laboratory procedure.” Cardiac catheterization and angiography were followed by transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography, and MRI, magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), and CT now provide exquisite anatomic detail and refined physiologic information.19–25

Given these advanced imaging techniques, and with more in the offing, has emphasis on the history, physical examination, electrocardiogram, chest x-ray, and echocardiogram become irrelevant? Intelligent selection of investigative procedures from an ever-increasing array requires far more sophisticated decisionmaking than was necessary when choices were limited to the electrocardiogram and chest x-ray. The basic clinical assessment provides the information necessary for most of these decisions. With increasing emphasis on the cost of medical care, it is likely that there will be a resurgence of interest in the inexpensive and safe clinical examination.26

### BOX 1.1 Five Basic Questions

1. Is the patient acyanotic or cyanotic? 2. Is pulmonary arterial blood flow increased or decreased? 3. Does the malformation originate in the left or right side of the

heart? 4. Which is the dominant ventricle? 5. Is pulmonary hypertension present?

Some additional points: The term natural history is not used. Julien Hoffman’s definition is relevant: “The natural history of any disease is a description of what happens to people with the disease who do not receive treatment for it.”27 Natural history is therefore not synonymous with unoperated, and unnatural history is not synonymous with postoperative. Nonsurgical therapeutic interventions can hardly be considered natural. A second point: differential diagnoses are not employed. Instead, each chapter ends with a summary that permits clinical recognition of the congenital anomaly covered in the chapter. These summaries bring together clinical highlights and serve as reminders for the reader’s convenience.

Accordingly, when abbreviations are used, they will first be defined for the reader’s convenience, but full terms will subsequently be used. New terms are not employed when old terms suffice. Acronyms are avoided.

We have tried to ensure that the material in this book is accessible to a broad audience. The terminology was assiduously addressed, and based on decades of personal experience, Dr. Perloff’s objective, so carefully transmitted to us, remains to excite interest and to be clearly understood.

title: Functional murmurs

paragraphs.text: 2 Functional Murmurs
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Practicing cardiology remains a powerful experience for the clinician. The ability to look, feel, and listen remains the most highly rewarding foundation of the diagnostic capability, nowhere more evident than in the assessment of subjects with congenital heart disease. The stethoscope is a lasting symbol of healing professions. Invented in 1816 by Laënnec in France, the word “stethoscope” originates from the Greek “stethos,” meaning “chest,” and “scope,” meaning “to look.”1 The original meaning of this classic tool has withstood the test of time, as primary diagnosis for cardiovascular disease has evolved with the stethoscope, the phonocardiogram, and cardiac ultrasound, all modalities that are discussed throughout this book.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Sounds produced by mechanical processes in the heart can be correlated with the presence or absence of disease. Most normal heart sounds occur during the closing of heart valves. Pathological murmurs occur where flow is made turbulent by the presence of abnormal pressure gradients between vascular structures, cardiac chambers and/or heart valves as they open and close. The timing, duration, pitch, intensity, location, and changes with hemodynamic maneuvers relate to the characteristics of the pressure changes from which they originate. In this chapter as in others, signal processing techniques,2 such as phonocardiogram recording, are used to illustrate heart sounds and murmurs.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Murmurs that occur in the absence of either morphologic or physiologic abnormalities of the heart or circulation have been called normal, innocent, functional, physiologic, or benign. These murmurs are common in children. The ability to differentiate functional from pathological murmurs is more consistent in children3 than in adults.4 The index of suspicion is the murmur itself in light of an otherwise normal auscultation, physical examination, and electrocardiogram.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Functional systolic and continuous murmurs unassociated with pathology are described below and shown in Box 2.1.5 Functional murmurs are never solely diastolic, with one exception: the transient left basal holodiastolic or middiastolic ductus arteriosus murmur sometimes heard during the first 3 or 4 days of life,6 where a valve-like structure at the pulmonary arterial end of the ductus (see Chapter 17) is held responsible for selective diastolic flow.6,7
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The normal vibratory midsystolic murmur was described by George F. Still in 1909 (Figs. 2.1 and 2.2).8 Still wrote, “It is heard usually just below the level of the nipple, and about halfway between the left margin of the sternum and the vertical nipple line....Its characteristic feature is a twanging sound very like that made by twanging a piece of tense string....Whatever may be its origin, I think it is clearly functional, that is to say, not due to any organic disease either congenital or acquired.”
paragraphs.heading: FUNCTIONAL SYSTOLIC MURMURS The Vibratory Systolic Murmur

paragraphs.text: Still’s murmur is seldom heard in infants9 but is prevalent after 3 years of age with diminishing frequency toward adolescence.10–13 The murmur ranges from grade 1 to 3/6 and is loudest between the apex and lower left sternal edge in the supine position.12,14–17 During exercise, excitement, or fever, the murmur intensifies (see Fig. 2.1).12 The quality is distinctive12,18—vibratory or buzzing with a uniform, medium, pure frequency (70 to 130 cycles per second)19 requiring the stethoscopic bell for best
paragraphs.heading: FUNCTIONAL SYSTOLIC MURMURS The Vibratory Systolic Murmur

paragraphs.text: assessment.14 The closest acoustic analogy is Still’s twanging of a taut rubber band or string (see earlier).20 The murmur begins shortly after the first heart sound and is typically confined to the first half of systole with a relatively long gap between the end of the murmur and the second heart sound (see Figs. 2.1 and 2.2).
paragraphs.heading: FUNCTIONAL SYSTOLIC MURMURS The Vibratory Systolic Murmur

paragraphs.text: The mechanism of Still’s murmur remains to be established. The pure medium frequency implies that a cardiac structure is set into periodic vibration during ventricular systole. Origin in the right side of the heart has been assigned to the pulmonary valve itself when “trigonoidation” of the leaflets results in periodic vibrations of the base of the cusps.13 A catheter across the pulmonary valve can tense the cusps and generate a transient purefrequency midsystolic murmur (Fig. 2.3B). The relatively low right ventricular ejection pressure and velocity are believed to cause the attachments of the pulmonary cusps to vibrate at a low to medium frequency. A murmur produced by a vibrating semilunar valve at its arterial attachment tends to be transmitted into the cavity of the concordant ventricle,21–23 which could account for the thoracic location of Still’s murmur between the apex and lower left sternal edge (i.e., topographically over the right ventricle). In children with Still’s murmur, Doppler echocardiography has identified systolic vibrations in the aortic valve and higher maximum acceleration of flow in the left ventricular outflow tract.17,24 However, a murmur originating in a vibrating aortic valve would be transmitted into the left ventricular cavity and heard best over the left ventricular impulse. Midsystolic murmurs in adults have been ascribed to high intraventricular velocities generated by vigorous left ventricular contraction associated with an increase in left ventricular mass.25 Origin of Still’s murmur has also been assigned to the left ventricular cavity, a location that is in accord with delayed response to the Valsalva maneuver.26 Left ventricular bands or false tendons (see Fig. 2.3A) are believed to vibrate periodically during ventricular systole and transmit their vibrations to the chest wall.27–29 A high percentage of patients with Still’s murmur reportedly have left ventricular bands, especially in the outflow tract.27–30 However, the prevalence of Still’s murmur declines from childhood to adolescence,12 ,13 whereas the prevalence of left ventricular bands is the same in children, adolescents, and adults.27,28,31 The incidence of Still’s murmur is believed to exceed the incidence of left ventricular bands,17 although incidence depends largely on the avidity with which bands are sought with echocardiography.
paragraphs.heading: FUNCTIONAL SYSTOLIC MURMURS The Vibratory Systolic Murmur

paragraphs.text: A functional systolic murmur in the main pulmonary artery is most prevalent in children, adolescents, and young adults.12,14,32 The murmur is midsystolic with maximum intensity in the second left intercostal space next to the sternum (Fig. 2.4), and ranges from barely audible to grade 3/6 in response to exercise, fever, or excitement. The frequency composition is mediumpitched and impure and best heard in the supine position with the stethoscopic diaphragm or moderate pressure of the bell during full held exhalation.12,14,33 The murmur represents normal ejection vibrations that reach the threshold of audibility from within the main pulmonary artery during right ventricular systole. The chest wall location is appropriate for origin in the pulmonary trunk, and intracardiac phonocardiograms record midsystolic murmurs within the pulmonary trunk in normal young subjects.33
paragraphs.heading: The Pulmonary Artery Systolic Murmur

paragraphs.heading: BOX 2.1 Functional Murmurs

paragraphs.text: These murmurs are commonly heard during pregnancy and in subjects with anemia or hyperthyroidism. Loss of thoracic kyphosis increases proximity of the pulmonary trunk to the chest wall and increases the incidence of pulmonary systolic murmurs in the second left interspace.34
paragraphs.heading: BOX 2.1 Functional Murmurs

paragraphs.text: impure, but most importantly, are distributed to the left and right anterior chest, axillae, and back. The similarity of frequency composition to breath sounds, the rapid respiratory rate of infants, and the widespread thoracic locations of pulmonary artery systolic murmurs cause these murmurs to be overlooked. Audibility is improved if respiration is temporarily arrested by pinching the nostrils while the infant sucks a pacifier. Auscultation is best carried out by examining the infant in both supine and prone positions and by using the stethoscopic diaphragm applied to the right and left anterior chest, back, and axillae. The murmurs are typically confined to neonates, are usually absent at the first well-baby examination, and seldom persist beyond 3 to 6 months of age.16,32,38 The transient branch pulmonary artery systolic murmur in normal neonates is indistinguishable from the peripheral murmur of fixed stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches (see Chapter 10). The analogy sheds light on the mechanism of production.32,36,37 The pulmonary trunk in the fetus is a relatively dilated domed structure because it receives the output of the high-pressure right ventricle. Proximal right and left pulmonary arteries arise from the pulmonary trunk as comparatively small lateral branches that receive a paucity of intrauterine blood flow. When the lungs expand at birth, the difference in size between the pulmonary trunk and its right and left branches transiently persists, especially in premature infants (Fig. 2.5).38 In addition to the disparity in size, the branches arise at relatively sharp angles from the inferior and posterior walls of the pulmonary trunk. These anatomic arrangements account for both the turbulence and the physiologic drop in systolic pressure from pulmonary trunk to proximal branches and for the branch pulmonary artery systolic murmur.32,37

paragraphs.text: Supraclavicular systolic arterial murmurs are typically heard in children and young adults, are always maximal above the clavicles, tend to be louder on the right, are generally bilateral, and are prominent in the suprasternal notch (Fig. 2.6).22,39 The weight of evidence assigns supraclavicular systolic murmurs to the aortic origins of major brachiocephalic arteries, especially the subclavians.40 Intensity can reach grade 4/6, may generate a thrill, and may be sufficient for radiation below the clavicles but with

paragraphs.text: distinct attenuation (see Fig. 2.6). The configuration of the supraclavicular systolic murmur is crescendo-decrescendo, the onset is abrupt, the duration is brief, and the timing is maximal in the first half or two-thirds of systole (see Fig. 2.6). The frequency composition is uneven, but the murmur is seldom noisy even when loud. Partial compression of the subclavian artery intensifies the murmur, whereas compression sufficient to obliterate the ipsilateral radial pulse has the opposite effect. Auscultation is most effectively carried out when the patient is sitting upright and looking straight ahead, with shoulders relaxed and forearms and hands on the lap (Fig. 2.7A).22,41 The stethoscopic bell is applied above the medial aspect of the right clavicle. The shoulders are then hyperextended with elbows brought sharply behind the back until shoulder girdle muscles are taut (see Fig. 2.7B). When this maneuver is done smoothly but rapidly, the supraclavicular murmur diminishes considerably or disappears altogether.41
paragraphs.heading: The Supraclavicular Systolic Murmur

paragraphs.text: The souffle is either confined to systole or is louder in systole even when continuous (see later). As the name implies, the mur - mur is heard over the breasts late in pregnancy but especially postpartum in lactating women ( Fig. 2.8). The systolic component was recognized by van den Bergh in 1908.42 The murmur begins distinctly after the first heart sound because sufficient time must elapse from left ventricular ejection to arrival at the artery of origin. The length of the murmur ranges from short (midsystolic), to long (up to the second heart sound), to beyond the second heart sound into diastole (continuous, see later).
paragraphs.heading: The Systolic Mammary Souffle

paragraphs.text: The most common form of midsystolic murmur in older adults is caused by fibrous or fibrocalcific thickening of the bases of unobstructed aortic cusps as they insert into the sinuses of
paragraphs.heading: Aortic Systolic Murmur in Older Adults

paragraphs.text: Valsalva (Fig. 2.9).43,44 As long as the fibrous or fibrocalcific thickening is confined to the base of the leaflets, the cusps move well, so there is no resistance to outflow. These structural alterations of aortic valves affect 20% to 25% of adults over age 65 years.22,43–48 The fibrous ridge-like thickenings that are initially confined to the base of the aortic cusps may subsequently extend to the free edges as fibrocalcification changes without commissural dysfunction. The accompanying murmur has been called the aortic sclerotic systolic murmur of older age. The aortic sclerotic murmur has been described to comprise two mechanisms. The murmur in the second right intercostal space is midsystolic, impure, grade 2 or 3/6, and originates within the aortic root (mixed-frequency ejection vibrations of non-laminar flow). The murmur heard over the left ventricular impulse is midsystolic, high-frequency musical, pure, grade 2 to 3/6, and originates from periodic vibrations of the stiffened bases of aortic cusps at the sinus of Valsalva attachments (see Fig. 2.9).21–23,43 These periodic vibrations have been recorded from aortic valve leaflets with M mode echocardiography.22 Intracardiac phonocardiography detects the musical high-frequency murmur within the left ventricular cavity, and

paragraphs.text: detects the harsh impure right basal murmur within the aortic root (Gallavardin dissociation) (see Fig. 2.9).22 There is reason to believe that the essential morphologic substrate for the development of aortic sclerosis on an inherently normal trileaflet aortic valve is cuspal inequality—a congenital variation of normal—as originally proposed by Roberts.49 The ideal aortic valve is equipped with cusps of identical size so that closing forces are equally distributed on the aortic surfaces of the three leaflets. At its inception, the process is functionally benign, although there is an association between aortic valve sclerosis and cardiovascular mortality and morbidity.45,50 Echocardiography can detect focal areas of increased echogenicity and thickening at aortic cusp attachments to the sinuses of Valsalva without restriction of leaflet motion.45

paragraphs.text: three cusps are illustrated. In fig. 3 only two cusps fill the orifice.” Functionally normal refers to a bicuspid aortic valve that has the trivial gradient and the trivial regurgitation inherent in a mechanism equipped with two rather than three leaflets. A bicuspid aortic valve at birth is either functionally normal, intrinsically stenotic, can become “thick and unyielding,” or conversely can become incompetent so that “blood which has entered the aorta is allowed to regurgitate into the ventricle,” as Thomas Peacock observed in 1858.52 It was William Osler in 1866 who called attention to the susceptibility of bicuspid aortic valves to infective endocarditis.53 A midsystolic murmur that is most prominent in the second right intercostal space in children or young adults arouses suspicion of a functionally normal bicuspid aortic valve, especially in males (relative male prevalence 70% to 75%).49 Auscultation should seek the confirmatory evidence of an aortic ejection sound that is most prominent at the apex.22,54 Additional evidence of a functionally normal bicuspid aortic valve is the soft high-frequency early diastolic murmur of bicuspid aortic regurgitation that adds materially to the diagnosis. The murmur is heard best when firm pressure of the stethoscopic diaphragm is applied at the mid left sternal edge during held exhalation as the patient sits and leans forward. Isometric exercise (clenched fists), squatting, and the Valsalva maneuver improve audibility.22,55
paragraphs.heading: The Functionally Normal Bicuspid Aortic Valve

paragraphs.text: The combination of a midsystolic murmur at the right base, an aortic ejection sound at the apex, and a soft high-frequency early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border in a young male establishes the diagnosis of bicuspid aortic valve. When the ejection sound is equivocal and the aortic regurgitation murmur is absent, clinical suspicion rests on the right basal midsystolic murmur alone. The echocardiogram then plays a pivotal role. The normal trileaflet aortic valve in the short-axis resembles the letter Y during diastole (Fig. 2.10A) and resembles an inverted triangle during systole.56 A congenitally bicuspid aortic valve appears as a single linear band in diastole (see Fig. 2.10B) and appears as a fish mouth in systole. Color flow imaging detects mild inaudible aortic regurgitation.

paragraphs.text: In 1915, Richard Cabot wrote:57
paragraphs.heading: The Cardiorespiratory Murmur

paragraphs.text: “Such murmurs may be heard under the left clavicle or below the angle of the left scapula, as well as near the apex of the heart– less often in other parts of the chest... Cardiorespiratory murmurs may be either systolic or diastolic, but in the vast majority of cases are systolic. The area over which they are audible is usually a very limited one. They are generally affected by a position and by respiration, and are heard most distinctly if not exclusively during inspiration, especially at the end of that act.”
paragraphs.heading: The Cardiorespiratory Murmur

paragraphs.text: Cardiorespiratory murmurs were known to Laënnec, but James Hope’s description is the most colorful.58 Hope described his examination of two university students:

paragraphs.text: The mechanism responsible for the cardiorespiratory murmur is unclear, but its benign nature as well as its location, timing, and relation to respiration remain as Cabot originally described.57
paragraphs.heading: The Cardiorespiratory Murmur

paragraphs.text: The venous hum was described by Potain in 186759 and is the most common type of functional continuous murmur. It is common in children and occurs in normal young adults,60,61 even in the absence of thyrotoxicosis, anemia, or pregnancy.22 Maximal

The hum may radiate widely and is often bilateral but is usually more prominent on the right (Fig. 2.11). A loud venous hum, especially in children, may radiate below the clavicles and be mistaken for a patent ductus arteriosus. Abolition of the hum by digital compression prevents this error (see Figs. 2.11 and 2.12). Intensity varies from faint to grade 6/6, and occasionally patients are subjectively and unpleasantly aware of a loud hum which is sensed as audible pulsatile tinnitus.62–64

paragraphs.text: A venous hum is best elicited with the patient sitting upright. The stethoscope held in the right hand of the examiner, the bell is applied to the medial aspect of the supraclavicular fossa (see Fig. 2.12A) while the examiner’s left hand grasps the patient’s chin from behind and pulls it tautly to the left and upward (see Fig. 2.12A).22 Occasionally, the hum develops or increases when the chin is simply tilted upward, and a prominent hum is sometimes audible without neck maneuvers and irrespective of position. In a child who is either sitting or supine, a venous hum may

The hum may appear when the child looks up at the examiner and may disappear when the child looks down at the stethoscope. The hum is reduced or abolished by digital compression of the ipsilateral internal jugular vein (see Fig. 2.12B), by removing the stretch on the neck as the head is returned to a neutral position, by the Valsalva maneuver, or by recumbency. The simplest procedure for abolishing the hum is compression of the deep jugular vein with the thumb of the free hand (see Fig. 2.12B). Compression causes instantaneous obliteration of the hum (see Fig. 2.11) which suddenly and transiently intensifies as pressure is released.22,61

paragraphs.text: The term hum does not necessarily characterize the quality of these cervical venous murmurs which can be rough and noisy, and are occasionally accompanied by a high-pitched whine.61 The hum is truly continuous (see Fig. 2.11), although typically louder in diastole, as is the case with venous continuous murmurs in general (Fig. 2.13). paragraphs.text: A second but far less common benign continuous murmur occurs during late pregnancy and early postpartum in normal lactating women. A consensus supports the view that the mammary souffle is arterial in origin,66–68 an opinion originally held by both van den Bergh42 and Morgan Jones.69 Origin in superficial veins of the breast has less credibility.70 The delay in onset, the accentuation in systole, the relatively high frequency, and persistence during the Valsalva maneuver are in accord with arterial origin.
paragraphs.heading: The Continuous Mammary Souffle

paragraphs.text: The continuous mammary souffle was included in Morgan- Jones’ 1951 book on Heart Disease in Pregnancy.69 Soufflare is Latin, meaning to blow. Maximal intensity of the souffle can be anywhere over either breast, but there is a tendency to be louder in the second or third right or left intercostal space, and occasionally the souffle is bilateral.68 A distinct gap between the first heart sound and the onset of the murmur represents the interval between ejection of blood from the left ventricle and arrival of blood at the artery that gives rise to the souffle.66–68 The murmur is typically louder in systole, as is usually the case with continuous murmurs of arterial origin, with the diastolic portion often fading completely before the subsequent first heart sound (see Figs. 2.13 and 2.14). The pitch may be relatively high, but the murmur is not musical.68 Audibility is best heard with the patient supine, and the murmur may vanish in the upright position.68 Light pressure with the stethoscope tends to augment the murmur and bring out its continuous features.67 Firm pressure with the stethoscope or

paragraphs.text: The location of a continuous mammary souffle may arouse suspicion of patent ductus arteriosus or of an arteriovenous fistula. However, the typical ductus murmur peaks at the second heart sound, whereas the mammary souffle peaks much earlier (see Fig. 2.14), and obliteration by local compression excludes patent ductus. An arteriovenous fistula may generate a continuous murmur that is maximal in systole and that attenuates with pressure, but the cycle-to-cycle or day-to-day variation of the mammary souffle and its invariable disappearance after termination of lactation resolve the issue.

paragraphs.text: Low-intensity cephalic murmurs which are usually continuous, less often systolic, are occasionally detected over the cranium of normal children under 4 years of age, especially in association with a febrile illness.16 These murmurs tend to be most prominent over the anterior fontanel, the temporal regions, or the orbits, and are best heard with the diaphragm of the stethoscope. Because auscultation is not routinely applied to the head, cephalic murmurs are overlooked. Their mechanism is unknown.

paragraphs.text: In summary, functional systolic murmurs include the vibratory murmur, the main and branch pulmonary artery murmur, the supraclavicular systolic murmur, the mammary souffle, the aortic systolic murmur of older adults, the murmur of a functionally normal bicuspid aortic valve, and the cardiorespiratory systolic murmur. All are midsystolic, except the mammary souffle, and are not loudest at the right base.22 Functional continuous murmurs include the venous hum, the continuous mammary souffle, and the continuous cephalic (cranial) murmur (see Box 2.1).

paragraphs.text: Cardiac auscultation remains a cornerstone in clinical assessment.71,72 As illustrated above, the skillful application of the stethoscope on the patient’s chest enables the clinical determination of the presence or absence of pathology and judicious use of complementary diagnostic investigation. The ability to correlate what one hears with what one visualizes with cardiac ultrasound can only enhance the use of evolving technologies as these achieve higher fidelity and become increasingly accessible.73,74

figures.caption: Fig. 2.9 (A) Illustration of Gallavardin dissociation of the two murmurs associated with fibrocalcific aortic stenosis of an inherently normal trileaflet aortic valve.75 The impure midsystolic murmur at the right base originates within the aortic root because of turbulence caused by the high velocity jet. The pure musical midsystolic murmur at the apex originates from periodic high frequency vibrations of the fibrocalcific aortic leaflets and radiates into the left ventricular cavity (LV). (B) Schematic illustrations that begin with the normal attachment of an aortic cusp to its sinus of Valsalva (normal). The initial alteration (mild) is a ridge-like fibrous thickening at the base of the aortic cusp as it inserts into its sinus. Calcium is subsequently deposited on the aortic surface of the leaflet (moderate), and ultimately extends to the free edge of the leaflet (severe), converting an inherently normal trileaflet valve into calcific aortic stenosis. (C) Schematic illustrations of a bicuspid aortic valve. The aortic cusp is thin and mobile yet domes during systole in a functionally normal bicuspid aortic valve (normal). The initial alteration (mild) is thickening of the leaflet tip with minimal restriction of mobility (mild). Calcium deposition occurs at the leaflet tip resulting in further restriction of mobility (moderate), eventually the calcification and fibrosis progresses proximally towards the cusp attachment to the sinus of Valsalva (severe) and the valve mobility is further reduced. The musical Gallavardin murmur does not occur in bicuspid aortic valve stenosis because leaflet mobility is not restricted to the same extent as in trileaflet aortic valve stenosis. Hence, there is an absence of the high-frequency fibrocalcific leaflet vibrations responsible for the musical quality of the murmur.

2 Functional Murmurs

Practicing cardiology remains a powerful experience for the clinician. The ability to look, feel, and listen remains the most highly rewarding foundation of the diagnostic capability, nowhere more evident than in the assessment of subjects with congenital heart disease. The stethoscope is a lasting symbol of healing professions. Invented in 1816 by Laënnec in France, the word “stethoscope” originates from the Greek “stethos,” meaning “chest,” and “scope,” meaning “to look.”1 The original meaning of this classic tool has withstood the test of time, as primary diagnosis for cardiovascular disease has evolved with the stethoscope, the phonocardiogram, and cardiac ultrasound, all modalities that are discussed throughout this book.

Sounds produced by mechanical processes in the heart can be correlated with the presence or absence of disease. Most normal heart sounds occur during the closing of heart valves. Pathological murmurs occur where flow is made turbulent by the presence of abnormal pressure gradients between vascular structures, cardiac chambers and/or heart valves as they open and close. The timing, duration, pitch, intensity, location, and changes with hemodynamic maneuvers relate to the characteristics of the pressure changes from which they originate. In this chapter as in others, signal processing techniques,2 such as phonocardiogram recording, are used to illustrate heart sounds and murmurs.

Murmurs that occur in the absence of either morphologic or physiologic abnormalities of the heart or circulation have been called normal, innocent, functional, physiologic, or benign. These murmurs are common in children. The ability to differentiate functional from pathological murmurs is more consistent in children3 than in adults.4 The index of suspicion is the murmur itself in light of an otherwise normal auscultation, physical examination, and electrocardiogram.

Functional systolic and continuous murmurs unassociated with pathology are described below and shown in Box 2.1.5 Functional murmurs are never solely diastolic, with one exception: the transient left basal holodiastolic or middiastolic ductus arteriosus murmur sometimes heard during the first 3 or 4 days of life,6 where a valve-like structure at the pulmonary arterial end of the ductus (see Chapter 17) is held responsible for selective diastolic flow.6,7

### FUNCTIONAL SYSTOLIC MURMURS The Vibratory Systolic Murmur

The normal vibratory midsystolic murmur was described by George F. Still in 1909 (Figs. 2.1 and 2.2).8 Still wrote, “It is heard usually just below the level of the nipple, and about halfway between the left margin of the sternum and the vertical nipple line....Its characteristic feature is a twanging sound very like that made by twanging a piece of tense string....Whatever may be its origin, I think it is clearly functional, that is to say, not due to any organic disease either congenital or acquired.”

Still’s murmur is seldom heard in infants9 but is prevalent after 3 years of age with diminishing frequency toward adolescence.10–13 The murmur ranges from grade 1 to 3/6 and is loudest between the apex and lower left sternal edge in the supine position.12,14–17 During exercise, excitement, or fever, the murmur intensifies (see Fig. 2.1).12 The quality is distinctive12,18—vibratory or buzzing with a uniform, medium, pure frequency (70 to 130 cycles per second)19 requiring the stethoscopic bell for best

assessment.14 The closest acoustic analogy is Still’s twanging of a taut rubber band or string (see earlier).20 The murmur begins shortly after the first heart sound and is typically confined to the first half of systole with a relatively long gap between the end of the murmur and the second heart sound (see Figs. 2.1 and 2.2).

The mechanism of Still’s murmur remains to be established. The pure medium frequency implies that a cardiac structure is set into periodic vibration during ventricular systole. Origin in the right side of the heart has been assigned to the pulmonary valve itself when “trigonoidation” of the leaflets results in periodic vibrations of the base of the cusps.13 A catheter across the pulmonary valve can tense the cusps and generate a transient purefrequency midsystolic murmur (Fig. 2.3B). The relatively low right ventricular ejection pressure and velocity are believed to cause the attachments of the pulmonary cusps to vibrate at a low to medium frequency. A murmur produced by a vibrating semilunar valve at its arterial attachment tends to be transmitted into the cavity of the concordant ventricle,21–23 which could account for the thoracic location of Still’s murmur between the apex and lower left sternal edge (i.e., topographically over the right ventricle). In children with Still’s murmur, Doppler echocardiography has identified systolic vibrations in the aortic valve and higher maximum acceleration of flow in the left ventricular outflow tract.17,24 However, a murmur originating in a vibrating aortic valve would be transmitted into the left ventricular cavity and heard best over the left ventricular impulse. Midsystolic murmurs in adults have been ascribed to high intraventricular velocities generated by vigorous left ventricular contraction associated with an increase in left ventricular mass.25 Origin of Still’s murmur has also been assigned to the left ventricular cavity, a location that is in accord with delayed response to the Valsalva maneuver.26 Left ventricular bands or false tendons (see Fig. 2.3A) are believed to vibrate periodically during ventricular systole and transmit their vibrations to the chest wall.27–29 A high percentage of patients with Still’s murmur reportedly have left ventricular bands, especially in the outflow tract.27–30 However, the prevalence of Still’s murmur declines from childhood to adolescence,12 ,13 whereas the prevalence of left ventricular bands is the same in children, adolescents, and adults.27,28,31 The incidence of Still’s murmur is believed to exceed the incidence of left ventricular bands,17 although incidence depends largely on the avidity with which bands are sought with echocardiography.

### The Pulmonary Artery Systolic Murmur

A functional systolic murmur in the main pulmonary artery is most prevalent in children, adolescents, and young adults.12,14,32 The murmur is midsystolic with maximum intensity in the second left intercostal space next to the sternum (Fig. 2.4), and ranges from barely audible to grade 3/6 in response to exercise, fever, or excitement. The frequency composition is mediumpitched and impure and best heard in the supine position with the stethoscopic diaphragm or moderate pressure of the bell during full held exhalation.12,14,33 The murmur represents normal ejection vibrations that reach the threshold of audibility from within the main pulmonary artery during right ventricular systole. The chest wall location is appropriate for origin in the pulmonary trunk, and intracardiac phonocardiograms record midsystolic murmurs within the pulmonary trunk in normal young subjects.33

### The Branch Pulmonary Artery Systolic Murmur

Branch pulmonary artery systolic murmurs are occasionally heard in normal neonates, especially premature neonates.32,35–37 These murmurs are typically grade 1 to 2/6, are medium-pitched, and

The similarity of frequency composition to breath sounds, the rapid respiratory rate of infants, and the widespread thoracic locations of pulmonary artery systolic murmurs cause these murmurs to be overlooked. Audibility is improved if respiration is temporarily arrested by pinching the nostrils while the infant sucks a pacifier. Auscultation is best carried out by examining the infant in both supine and prone positions and by using the stethoscopic diaphragm applied to the right and left anterior chest, back, and axillae. The murmurs are typically confined to neonates, are usually absent at the first well-baby examination, and seldom persist beyond 3 to 6 months of age.16,32,38 The transient branch pulmonary artery systolic murmur in normal neonates is indistinguishable from the peripheral murmur of fixed stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches (see Chapter 10). The analogy sheds light on the mechanism of production.32,36,37 The pulmonary trunk in the fetus is a relatively dilated domed structure because it receives the output of the high-pressure right ventricle. Proximal right and left pulmonary arteries arise from the pulmonary trunk as comparatively small lateral branches that receive a paucity of intrauterine blood flow. When the lungs expand at birth, the difference in size between the pulmonary trunk and its right and left branches transiently persists, especially in premature infants (Fig. 2.5).38 In addition to the disparity in size, the branches arise at relatively sharp angles from the inferior and posterior walls of the pulmonary trunk. These anatomic arrangements account for both the turbulence and the physiologic drop in systolic pressure from pulmonary trunk to proximal branches and for the branch pulmonary artery systolic murmur.32,37

### The Supraclavicular Systolic Murmur

Supraclavicular systolic arterial murmurs are typically heard in children and young adults, are always maximal above the clavicles, tend to be louder on the right, are generally bilateral, and are prominent in the suprasternal notch (Fig. 2.6).22,39 The weight of evidence assigns supraclavicular systolic murmurs to the aortic origins of major brachiocephalic arteries, especially the subclavians.40 Intensity can reach grade 4/6, may generate a thrill, and may be sufficient for radiation below the clavicles but with

LV

distinct attenuation (see Fig. 2.6). The configuration of the supraclavicular systolic murmur is crescendo-decrescendo, the onset is abrupt, the duration is brief, and the timing is maximal in the first half or two-thirds of systole (see Fig. 2.6). The frequency composition is uneven, but the murmur is seldom noisy even when loud. Partial compression of the subclavian artery intensifies the murmur, whereas compression sufficient to obliterate the ipsilateral radial pulse has the opposite effect. Auscultation is most effectively carried out when the patient is sitting upright and looking straight ahead, with shoulders relaxed and forearms and hands on the lap (Fig. 2.7A).22,41 The stethoscopic bell is applied above the medial aspect of the right clavicle. The shoulders are then hyperextended with elbows brought sharply behind the back until shoulder girdle muscles are taut (see Fig. 2.7B). When this maneuver is done smoothly but rapidly, the supraclavicular murmur diminishes considerably or disappears altogether.41

### The Systolic Mammary Souffle

The souffle is either confined to systole or is louder in systole even when continuous (see later). As the name implies, the mur - mur is heard over the breasts late in pregnancy but especially postpartum in lactating women ( Fig. 2.8). The systolic component was recognized by van den Bergh in 1908.42 The murmur begins distinctly after the first heart sound because sufficient time must elapse from left ventricular ejection to arrival at the artery of origin. The length of the murmur ranges from short (midsystolic), to long (up to the second heart sound), to beyond the second heart sound into diastole (continuous, see later).

These structural alterations of aortic valves affect 20% to 25% of adults over age 65 years.22,43–48 The fibrous ridge-like thickenings that are initially confined to the base of the aortic cusps may subsequently extend to the free edges as fibrocalcification changes without commissural dysfunction. The accompanying murmur has been called the aortic sclerotic systolic murmur of older age. The aortic sclerotic murmur has been described to comprise two mechanisms. The murmur in the second right intercostal space is midsystolic, impure, grade 2 or 3/6, and originates within the aortic root (mixed-frequency ejection vibrations of non-laminar flow). The murmur heard over the left ventricular impulse is midsystolic, high-frequency musical, pure, grade 2 to 3/6, and originates from periodic vibrations of the stiffened bases of aortic cusps at the sinus of Valsalva attachments (see Fig. 2.9).21–23,43 These periodic vibrations have been recorded from aortic valve leaflets with M mode echocardiography.22 Intracardiac phonocardiography detects the musical high-frequency murmur within the left ventricular cavity, and

At its inception, the process is functionally benign, although there is an association between aortic valve sclerosis and cardiovascular mortality and morbidity.45,50 Echocardiography can detect focal areas of increased echogenicity and thickening at aortic cusp attachments to the sinuses of Valsalva without restriction of leaflet motion.45

A bicuspid aortic valve at birth is either functionally normal, intrinsically stenotic, can become “thick and unyielding,” or conversely can become incompetent so that “blood which has entered the aorta is allowed to regurgitate into the ventricle,” as Thomas Peacock observed in 1858.52 It was William Osler in 1866 who called attention to the susceptibility of bicuspid aortic valves to infective endocarditis.53 A midsystolic murmur that is most prominent in the second right intercostal space in children or young adults arouses suspicion of a functionally normal bicuspid aortic valve, especially in males (relative male prevalence 70% to 75%).49 Auscultation should seek the confirmatory evidence of an aortic ejection sound that is most prominent at the apex.22,54 Additional evidence of a functionally normal bicuspid aortic valve is the soft high-frequency early diastolic murmur of bicuspid aortic regurgitation that adds materially to the diagnosis. The murmur is heard best when firm pressure of the stethoscopic diaphragm is applied at the mid left sternal edge during held exhalation as the patient sits and leans forward. Isometric exercise (clenched fists), squatting, and the Valsalva maneuver improve audibility.22,55

The combination of a midsystolic murmur at the right base, an aortic ejection sound at the apex, and a soft high-frequency early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border in a young male establishes the diagnosis of bicuspid aortic valve. ### The Cardiorespiratory Murmur

In 1915, Richard Cabot wrote:57

“Such murmurs may be heard under the left clavicle or below the angle of the left scapula, as well as near the apex of the heart– less often in other parts of the chest... They are generally affected by a position and by respiration, and are heard most distinctly if not exclusively during inspiration, especially at the end of that act.”

### The Continuous Mammary Souffle

A second but far less common benign continuous murmur occurs during late pregnancy and early postpartum in normal lactating women. A consensus supports the view that the mammary souffle is arterial in origin,66–68 an opinion originally held by both van den Bergh42 and Morgan Jones.69 Origin in superficial veins of the breast has less credibility.70 The delay in onset, the accentuation in systole, the relatively high frequency, and persistence during the Valsalva maneuver are in accord with arterial origin.

The continuous mammary souffle was included in Morgan- Jones’ 1951 book on Heart Disease in Pregnancy.69 Soufflare is Latin, meaning to blow. Maximal intensity of the souffle can be anywhere over either breast, but there is a tendency to be louder in the second or third right or left intercostal space, and occasionally the souffle is bilateral.68 A distinct gap between the first heart sound and the onset of the murmur represents the interval between ejection of blood from the left ventricle and arrival of blood at the artery that gives rise to the souffle.66–68 The murmur is typically louder in systole, as is usually the case with continuous murmurs of arterial origin, with the diastolic portion often fading completely before the subsequent first heart sound (see Figs. 2.13 and 2.14). The pitch may be relatively high, but the murmur is not musical.68 Audibility is best heard with the patient supine, and the murmur may vanish in the upright position.68 Light pressure with the stethoscope tends to augment the murmur and bring out its continuous features.67 Firm pressure with the stethoscope or

paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Inversus: Reverse or opposite. Situs inversus: Opposite or reverse of normal (Figs. 3.2 and 3.3). Ambiguus: Uncertain, indeterminant. Situs ambiguus: Uncertain, indeterminant, or ambiguous position. Cardiac displacement: A secondary shift in intrathoracic cardiac
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Dextrocardia in situs inversus was known to the anatomistsurgeon Marco Aurelio Severino in 1643 and was one of the first recognized congenital malformations of the heart.1 Nearly a century and a half elapsed before Matthew Baillie’s account of “complete transposition in the human subject, of the thoracic and abdominal viscera, to the opposite side from what is natural.”2 In 1958 Thomas Peacock indicated that “the heart may be congenitally misplaced in various ways, occupying either an unusual position with the thorax, or being situated external to that cavity.”3 In 1901 Paltauf published remarkable illustrations that distinguished the various types of dextrocardia,4 and in 1928 the first useful classification of cardiac malpositions was proposed.5 Subsequent observations by Lichtman6 and by de la Cruz7 shed light on the embryologic bases of the malpositions, and the landmark observations of van Praagh confirmed the validity of those assumptions.8 Campbell’s diagrams in the 1950s and 1960s9–11 and Elliott’s radiologic classification in 196612 set the stage for the clinical recognition of cardiac malpositions.

paragraphs.text: Cardiac malpositions, which have a prevalence of 0.10 per 1000 live births,13 refer to hearts that are located abnormally within the thoracic cavity or that are located outside the thoracic cavity— ectopia cordis.14 Cardiac midline and lateral defects occur along three geometric axes: anterior-posterior, dorsal-ventral, and leftright.15 Genes expressed in dorsal midline cells coordinate the development of the three embryonic axes, driving the cardiac tube to loop in the appropriate direction relative to body axes. The left-right axis is established at approximately the 18th day after fertilization.15 Both bilateral left-sidedness and bilateral right-sidedness have been reported in members of the same family, implying that the two conditions are different manifestations of a primary defect in lateralization.16

paragraphs.text: The first section of this chapter deals with the three basic cardiac malpositions in the presence of bilateral asymmetry. The second section of the chapter deals with cardiac malpositions in the presence of bilateral symmetry. Certain organs or structures are in fact bilateral but asymmetrical such as the bronchi and lungs. Certain essentially unilateral organs such as the liver are transverse. Parts of certain structures such as the atrial appendages are symmetrical, while the remainder of the atria are morphologically different.
