title: Congenital pulmonary stenosis and regurgitation

paragraphs.text: 10 10 Congenital Pulmonary Stenosis and Regurgitation
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis was described in 1761 by John Baptist Morgagni.1 In 1941, McAlister Gregg, an Australian ophthalmologist, described a relationship between maternal rubella and congenital abnormalities in offspring.2 What came to be known as the rubella syndrome consists of stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches with patent ductus arteriosus.3,4 Subinfundibular stenosis or double-chambered right ventricle was described by Thomas Peacock who recognized the murmur in 1858.5 Obstructing muscle bundles within the right ventricular cavity were the subject of Sir Arthur Keith’s Hunterian lecture in 1909.6 Pulmonary artery stenosis (supravalvular) was described by Oppenheimer in 1938.7
paragraphs.heading: HISTORICAL NOTES

paragraphs.text: William Osler described pulmonary regurgitation in The Principles and Practice of Medicine (1892).8 This rare affection is occasionally due to a congenital malformation, particularly fusion of the two segments ... The condition is extremely rare and of little practical significance. The distinctive diastolic murmur of low-pressure pulmonary regurgitation was characterized in 1910,9 and in 1936, isolated congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation was reported with a review of the literature.10 Maude Abbott’s necropsy study of 1000 cases of congenital heart disease included two examples of isolated congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation.11 In 1955, the first clinical diagnosis was made in an asymptomatic 24-year-old medical student.12
paragraphs.heading: HISTORICAL NOTES

paragraphs.text: This chapter is concerned with isolated obstruction of the pulmonary valve or right ventricular outflow tract and pulmonary valve regurgitation as an isolated congenital malformation. It does not include pulmonary stenosis that occurs in conjunction with complex congenital heart disease or pulmonary regurgitation associated with pulmonary hypertension.
paragraphs.heading: HISTORICAL NOTES

paragraphs.text: Typical mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis is relatively common with a prevalence as high as 10% of cases of congenital heart disease.13,14 Sex distribution is equal or with female prevalence.14 This is also the case in dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis.15
paragraphs.heading: PULMONARY STENOSIS Incidence and Prevalence

paragraphs.text: Congenital obstruction to right ventricular outflow in hearts with two non-inverted ventricles originates in, below or above the pulmonary valve. Three morphologic types of pulmonary stenosis involve the pulmonary valve: (1) typical mobile dome-shaped, (2) dysplastic, and (3) bicuspid. Dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis is characterized by a thin mobile valve mechanism with a narrow central opening at its apex (Fig. 10.1). Three rudimentary raphes extend from the central opening to the wall of the pulmonary artery, but separate leaflets and separate commissures cannot be identified. Pinpoint dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis in neonates is sometimes referred to as functional pulmonary atresia (see Fig. 10.1, lower, A and B). The pulmonary trunk is consistently dilated because an inherent medial abnormality16 is coupled
paragraphs.heading: Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: with the mobile dome-shaped valve, but not with its functional state (see Fig. 10.1). The jet from the stenotic valve breaks up upon striking the apex of the pulmonary trunk. The pressure component of total energy increases with a proportionate increase pressure in the left branch (Fig. 10.2A).17 The physics of jet dispersion is believed to account for the larger size of the left branch. Calcification of a dome-shaped stenotic pulmonary valve is exceptional and is reserved for older patients.18 Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis is much less common and is characterized by myomatous thickening of three separate but poorly mobile leaflets without commissural fusion (Fig. 10.3 and Box 10.1).19,20 Bicuspid pulmonary valve stenosis is a feature of Fallot’s tetralogy (see Chapter 13). Isolated bicuspid pulmonary valves are rare and are of little or no functional significance.
paragraphs.heading: Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: Subvalvular pulmonary stenosis can be infundibular or subinfundibular. The infundibular variety is caused by anterior and rightward deviation (malalignment) of the infundibular septum and is dealt with in Chapter 13. Secondary hypertrophic infundibular pulmonary stenosis accompanies—is secondary to—severe pulmonary valve stenosis (Figs. 10.4 and 10.5). Stenosis of the ostium of the infundibulum is a rare form of fixed obstruction to right ventricular outflow (Figs. 10.6 and 10.7). Subinfundibular stenosis or double-chambered right ventricle is a rare form of congenital obstruction to right ventricular outflow. Obstructing muscle bundles within the right ventricular cavity result in a double-chambered right ventricle; the right ventricle is hence divided into a high-pressure inlet portion and a low-pressure outlet portion by normal or anomalous muscle bundles21,22 or by apical trabecular muscle sequestered from the rest of the right ventricle.23 The degree of obstruction varies from nil to severe to virtually complete.22 Double-chambered right ventricle usually coexists with a ventricular septal defect.21,22
paragraphs.heading: Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary artery stenosis (supravalvular) is caused by narrowing of the pulmonary trunk, its bifurcation, or its primary or intrapulmonary branches (Figs. 10.8 and 10.9).24 Stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches usually occurs as an isolated malformation24 and can be unilateral or bilateral, single or multiple, and segmental or tubular (see Figs. 10.8 and 10.9).24 Intrapulmonary arteries distal to the stenoses tend to be dilated (see Figs. 10.8 and 10.9). Rarely, a membranous form of obstruction occurs immediately above the valve.24
paragraphs.heading: Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: Neonates, especially premature, normally exhibit a disparity in size between the pulmonary trunk and its proximal branches. Angulations at the origins of the branches cause a drop in systolic pressure in the absence of morphologic pulmonary artery stenosis (see Chapter 2 and Fig. 2.4).25,26 The small pulmonary trunk and small proximal branches in Fallot’s tetralogy are discussed in Chapter 15. In Williams syndrome, bilateral stenosis of pulmonary artery branches is associated with supravalvular aortic stenosis (see Chapter 7).27 Experimental constriction of the pulmonary trunk in fetal lambs results in thin-walled intrapulmonary resistance vessels.28
paragraphs.heading: Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: The physiological consequences of pulmonary stenosis result from increased resistance to right ventricular discharge. Systolic pressure is elevated proximal to the obstruction and is normal or reduced distally. Pulmonary artery stenosis causes an increase in systolic pressure in the pulmonary trunk which is proximal to the obstruction (Fig. 10.10). Valvular and subvalvular pulmonary stenosis increase the systolic pressure in the right ventricle that is

Accordingly, each replicated normal-sized myocyte is paired with its own capillary, so myocyte/capillary ratio (capillary density) is normal. However, a morphologic right ventricle is perfused by a morphologic right coronary artery which imposes an inherent limitation.
paragraphs.heading: BOX 10.1 Congenitally Dysplastic Pulmonary Valve

paragraphs.text: Children and young adults with mild to moderate pulmonary valve stenosis have normal or near-normal right ventricular function and can increase their cardiac output with exercise.31 In severe pulmonary valve stenosis, however, stroke volume and cardiac output are fixed.32 Systolic contraction of hypertrophied infundibular muscle (see Fig. 10.4) is reinforced by exercise.31
paragraphs.heading: BOX 10.1 Congenitally Dysplastic Pulmonary Valve

paragraphs.text: Pressure overload of the right ventricle can result in systolic and diastolic dysfunction of the left ventricle.33,34 Systolic dysfunction has been ascribed to chronic underfilling of the left ventricle,

paragraphs.text: Patients with isolated pulmonary stenosis tend to have a favorable long-term prognosis35 with little progression of disease in
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: PT
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: those with mild valvar pulmonary stenosis.36 Even so, great strides have been made in diagnostic capabilities and therapeutic options for patients with obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract further optimizing outcomes.37,38
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Familial recurrence of isolated pulmonary valve stenosis is uncommon if not rare (Fig. 10.11).39–42 In dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis, the converse is the case.19 Some family members have a dysplastic valve, while others have a mobile dome-shaped valve.19 Familial Noonan syndrome frequently occurs with dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis and has appeared in three generations.43,44 Successful pregnancy is possible in females with Noonan syndrome.45 Familial pulmonary artery stenosis occurs as an isolated anomaly or with coexisting supravalvular aortic stenosis. Members of the same family may have either or both anomalies.
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Genetic anomalies have been associated with pulmonary stenosis with and without Noonan syndrome. Cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome occurs sporadically with multiple congenital anomalies where pulmonary stenosis is more common in individuals with a BRAF mutation.46 PTPN11 mutations cause LEOPARD syndrome and Noonan syndrome, both of which are part of a family of autosomal dominant syndromes termed “RASopathies,” which are developmental diseases caused by mutations in genes encoding for signal transducers of the RAS-MAPK cascade.47,48 Cardiac defects occur in 80% of these with worst outcomes described in those with Noonan syndrome and pulmonary stenosis who carry the PTPN11 mutations.48
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Normal birth weights and normal growth and development are characteristic of mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis. However, in Noonan syndrome with dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis, growth and development are poor.15,19,49 Pulmonary artery stenosis is associated with low birth weights and retarded physical and mental development in the rubella syndrome and in Williams syndrome (see Chapter 7).3,50
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Neonates with pinpoint pulmonary valve stenosis experience rapidly progressive cardiac failure. However, the majority of patients with mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis experience little or no difficulty in infancy and childhood.36 In a review of 69 cases, the average age at death was 26 years, seven patients survived to age 50 years, and three survived to 70 and 75 years. In 21 adults, the average follow-up was 50 years.51 There are examples of survival into the sixth, seventh, and eighth decade,52–56 with one patient reaching 78 years.52 Longevity depends on three variables: (1) the initial severity of stenosis, (2) whether a given
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: degree of stenosis remains constant or progresses, and (3) whether the function of the afterloaded right ventricle is preserved.32,36,57
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: The normal pulmonary valve orifice increases linearly with age and body surface area.58 The orifice of a stenotic mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve increases with age, but not necessarily at the rate of somatic growth.36,58–60 Mild pulmonary valve stenosis in infancy usually remains mild,61 but moderate to severe pulmonary stenosis tends to progress.54 Stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches is not progressive. Fibrous thickening and occasionally calcification are responsible for increasing the degree of stenosis in older adults.
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Equivalent degrees of pulmonary stenosis may handicap one patient in childhood but leave another relatively free of symptoms in adulthood. It is not surprising that mild pulmonary stenosis is asymptomatic, but it is surprising that an appreciable number of patients with moderate to severe pulmonary stenosis claim to be virtually asymptomatic. Patients with right ventricular systolic pressures between 50 and 100 mm Hg include a New Zealand long-distance swimmer, a long-distance runner, and an English hockey captain.62 My patients include a 17-yearold boy who played baseball despite a right ventricular systolic pressure of nearly 200 mm Hg, a 32-year-old male who had run the quarter mile in high school despite a right ventricular systolic pressure of 75 mm Hg, and a female with a right ventricular pressure of nearly 200 mm Hg who worked full-time and had recurrent ascites for 7 years before death at age 60 years. Dyspnea and fatigue are mild as long as the right ventricle maintains a normal stroke volume at rest and augments its stroke volume with exercise.32,57 However, relatively asymptomatic patients can deteriorate rapidly. Cardiac output is inadequate even at rest when the hemodynamic burden imposed on the right ventricle leads to right ventricular failure, the commonest cause of death.53
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Giddiness and light-headedness with effort prefigure syncope.62 Children as well as adults occasionally experience the chest pain of right ventricular myocardial ischemia.56,63 A 3-year-old with severe pulmonary artery stenosis died during an episode of chest pain and at necropsy had infarction of the right ventricular free wall and interventricular septum.63 Sudden death has been associated with right ventricular infarction and an abnormal right coronary artery.64 Dilated thin-walled intrapulmonary artery aneurysms distal to the stenoses of pulmonary artery branches (see Fig. 10.9B) are sources of hemoptyses that can be intermittent and mild or recurrent and brisk.24
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Severe pulmonary stenosis is accompanied by giant jugular venous A waves (Fig. 10.12) that patients are subjectively

A 13-year-old girl with pulmonary valve stenosis and congenital complete heart block was aware of intermittent amplification of A waves as her right atrium randomly contracted against a closed tricuspid valve, and a 15-year-old boy was unpleasantly aware of intermittent amplification of jugular venous A waves caused by premature ventricular beats.
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis is a substrate for infective endocarditis54 that can induce a medical valvotomy when tissue is interrupted and orifice size increases.62 Jet lesions in pulmonary artery stenosis can serve as substrates for infective endarteritis.24
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Six physical appearances are relevant in patients with congenital pulmonary stenosis: (1) the round bloated facies in infants with mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis, (2) Noonan syndrome, (3) the rubella syndrome, (4) Williams syndrome, (5) Alagille syndrome, and (6) the Cornelia de Lange syndrome.
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: Infants with mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis occasionally have chubby round bloated facies with highly colored cheeks (Fig. 10.13A) and well-developed fat deposits.62 The digits may be erythematous or frankly red in response to a small or intermittent right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale. Noonan syndrome45,65,66 (see Fig. 10.13C) is characterized by short stature, webbed neck, pterygium colli, ptosis, hypertelorism, lymphedema, low-set ears, low anterior and posterior hairlines, flat or shield chest, pectus excavatum or carinatum, hyperelastic skin, inguinal hernia, nevi, dystrophic nails, micrognathia, hypospadias, and small undescended or cryptorchid testes,44,65 foramen ovale (see Chapter 12).
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: About one-third of Noonan patients are intellectually disabled, and approximately two-thirds have congenital heart disease, especially dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis (60%) or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (20%).65,67,68 Mild pulmonary stenosis in patients with Noonan syndrome is typically nonprogressive.69 Malignant tumor development is a complication encountered in other RASopathies, though the neoplastic risks and incidence of malignant tumors are less clearly defined in Noonan syndrome and related disorders of the Noonan spectrum.70
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: A B

paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: The rubella syndrome is characterized by cataracts, retinopathy, deafness, hypotonia, dermatoglyphic abnormalities, and intellectual disability.71 Height and weight are usually normal for age despite intrauterine growth retardation. Stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches and patent ductus arteriosus (see Chapter 17) are the most frequent types of coexisting congenital heart disease.71
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: Williams syndrome includes a small chin, large mouth, patulous lips, blunt upturned nose, wide-set eyes, broad forehead, baggy cheeks, and malformed teeth (see Chapter 7). The most frequent coexisting congenital heart disease is pulmonary artery stenosis with supravalvular aortic stenosis (see Chapter 7).
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: Alagille syndrome, also called arteriohepatic dysplasia or the Alagille-Watson syndrome, is an autosomal dominant disorder with abnormalities of liver, eyes, kidneys, and skeleton.72,73 Facial appearance is characterized by a prominent overhanging forehead, deep-set eyes, and a small pointed chin (see Fig. 10.13B).72–74 The most frequent coexisting congenital heart disease is stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches.73
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: Cornelia de Lange syndrome expresses itself as low birth weight; slow growth; small stature; microcephaly; thin eyebrows that meet at midline; long eyelashes; short upturned nose; thin, downturned lips; hirsutism; small hands and feet; in-curved fifth fingers; cleft palate; and missing limbs or portions of limbs. The incidence of pulmonary valve stenosis is reportedly 39%.75
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary stenosis also occurs in the LEOPARD syndrome that is characterized by multiple lentigines and café-au-lait spots.76
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: E
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: When severe pulmonary stenosis is accompanied by right ventricular failure, especially with coexisting left ventricular dysfunction, the arterial pulse is reduced. Asymmetry of right and left brachial and carotid arterial pulses (right greater than left) is a feature of supravalvular aortic stenosis that may accompany stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches (see Chapter 7).
paragraphs.heading: The Arterial Pulse

paragraphs.text: The jugular venous A wave is distinctive, increasing progressively as the stenosis increases (Fig. 10.14; see also Fig. 10.12A), culminating in a giant A wave that leaps to the eye, towering above and dwarfing the other waves of the venous pulse.13 Powerful right atrial contraction generates a giant A wave via the superior vena cava and a presystolic liver pulse via the inferior cava. With the advent of right ventricular failure and tricuspid regurgitation, the large A wave is accompanied by an increase in the V wave. The liver then manifests presystolic and systolic pulsations.
paragraphs.heading: The Jugular Venous Pulse

paragraphs.text: The thrill associated with pulmonary valve stenosis is maximum in the second left intercostal space with radiation upward and to the left because the intrapulmonary jet is directed upward and toward the left pulmonary artery (see Fig. 10.2A).17 When secondary hypertrophic subpulmonary stenosis coexists, the thrill is maximum in the third or fourth left intercostal space (see Fig. 10.4).
paragraphs.heading: Precordial Movement and Palpation

paragraphs.text: Palpation of the right ventricular impulse is best achieved by applying the fingertips between the ribs along the left sternal edge during full held exhalation or when a single fingertip is applied against the diaphragm in the subxiphoid area.77,78 The subxiphoid technique is especially useful in infants because rapid respiratory excursions interfere with parasternal palpation. In severe pulmonary valve stenosis, the right ventricular impulse is forceful and sustained and is detected up to and including the third intercostal space.77–79 Infundibular pulmonary stenosis relegates the high-pressure zone to the inflow portion of the right
paragraphs.heading: Precordial Movement and Palpation

paragraphs.text: A
paragraphs.heading: Precordial Movement and Palpation

paragraphs.text: V
paragraphs.heading: Precordial Movement and Palpation

paragraphs.text: ventricle, so the accompanying impulse is assigned to the fourth and fifth left intercostal spaces. Subinfundibular stenosis is accompanied by a deceptively unimpressive right ventricular impulse confined to the fifth interspace or subxiphoid area. The pulmonary trunk is necessarily distal to the stenosis and cannot be palpated despite conspicuous dilatation.
paragraphs.heading: Precordial Movement and Palpation

paragraphs.text: A presystolic impulse along the lower-left sternal border and in the subxiphoid area (see Fig. 10.12B) indicates presystolic distention of the right ventricle in response to the increased force of right atrial contraction that is also responsible for the large jugular venous A wave (see Fig. 10.12A). A prominent pulmonary ejection sound is occasionally palpable in the second left intercostal space during held exhalation.
paragraphs.heading: Precordial Movement and Palpation

paragraphs.text: A pulmonary ejection sound coincides with abrupt cephalad movement of the mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve (see Figs. 10.1B, upper, and 10.4) and is therefore an important sign in the auscultatory characterization of right ventricular outflow obstruction (Fig. 10.15).78,80 An ejection sound does not occur with dysplastic pulmonary valves that move poorly if at all19 or with fixed subvalvular or pulmonary artery stenosis.78 An ejection

paragraphs.text: sound can also originate in a functionally normal bicuspid pulmonary valve.81 The sound is recognized by its high-pitched clicking quality, by its maximum intensity in the second left intercostal space and by its distinctive selective decrease during inspiration (Figs. 10.16 through 10.18).78,82,83 The inspiratory decrease is related to the reduced cephalad movement available to the mobile valve as the right ventricle contracts.82 The inspiratory increase in right atrial contractile force is transmitted into the right ventricle and onto the undersurface of the mobile pulmonary valve that moves into a relatively cephalad position.84 Additional cephalad movement is necessarily reduced, so the ejection sound is reduced or vanishes altogether.82 Conversely, the right atrial contractile force decreases during expiration, leaving the mobile pulmonary valve in a slack position, so right ventricular contraction induces maximum cephalad movement and maximum intensity of the ejection sound.82
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: The interval between the first heart sound and the ejection sound varies inversely with the degree of stenosis (see Fig. 10.15).80,85 As severity increases, the velocity of right ventricular contraction increases, the pulmonary valve opens earlier, and the ejection sound occurs earlier and merges with the first heart sound (see Fig. 10.15) but retains its distinctive respiratory variation that distinguishes it from a loud first heart sound.85,86 Accordingly, a pulmonary ejection sound that occurs at a welldefined interval after the first heart sound is a sign of mild pulmonary valve stenosis, and an ejection sound that merges with the first heart sound is a sign of severe pulmonary stenosis. Fibrosis and calcification in older patients impair mobility, so the ejection sound decreases or disappears altogether.
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: The maximum precordial site is the second left intercostal space (see Figs. 10.16 through 10.18) that topographically overlies the pulmonary trunk and coincides with the location of the murmur recorded by intracardiac phonocardiography (see Fig. 10.16B).78 Prominence of the murmur in the third left intercostal space occurs with secondary hypertrophic subpulmonary stenosis (Fig. 10.19B; see also Fig 10.4). The murmur radiates upward and to the left (see Fig. 10.17) because the intrapulmonary jet is directed upward and to the left (see Fig. 10.2A). Loud systolic murmurs radiate into the suprasternal notch and the base of the neck, especially the left side. Intensity varies directly with the degree of obstruction, but intensity per se is not necessarily an index of severity. In neonates with pinpoint pulmonary stenosis, the murmur is deceptively soft (see Fig. 10.1 lower A, B). Grade 3/6 murmurs are features of mild pulmonary stenosis (see Fig. 10.16), and grade 3/6 to 6/6 murmurs are features of moderate to severe pulmonary stenosis (see Figs. 10.17 through 10.19).
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: The severity determines the duration of right ventricular ejection that in turn determines the duration of the systolic murmur. However, the murmur of pinpoint pulmonary stenosis (see Fig. 10.1, lower) is disarmingly soft. Murmurs at nonprecordial thoracic sites accompany pulmonary artery stenosis and in neonates and infants are easily overlooked or lost in the rapid breath sounds.
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: The length of the murmur relative to the aortic component of the second heart sound permits comparison of the duration of right and left ventricular ejection (see Fig. 10.15). When pulmonary stenosis is mild, right ventricle remains normal, so a symmetric systolic murmur ends before the aortic component of the second sound (see Figs. 10.15 and 10.16).86 When stenosis is moderate, the murmur ends at or slightly after the aortic component of the second sound which remains audible (see Figs. 10.15 and 10.17).86 When stenosis is severe, the murmur extends beyond the aortic component which is partially or completely obscured (see Figs. 10.15, 10.18, and 10.19).86 With a still greater increase in severity, the murmur lengthens further, peaks later in systole, and assumes an asymmetric kite-shape.85,86 Fig. 10.15 illustrates the relationship between the duration and configuration of the systolic murmur and the degree of pulmonary stenosis. paragraphs.text: Stenosis of the ostium of the infundibulum (see Figs. 10.6 and 10.7) is accompanied by a murmur that is maximal in the third and fourth left intercostal spaces (see Fig. 10.19).13,86 Subinfundibular stenosis assigns the murmur still lower—to the fourth or fifth left intercostal space.87
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: Several types of diastolic murmurs occur, although rarely, in pulmonary valve stenosis. A low-intensity atrial systolic murmur is attributed to presystolic flow across the pulmonary valve (Fig. 10.20A).80 Powerful right atrial contraction generates a giant A wave that exceeds the diastolic pressure in the pulmonary trunk, so the pulmonary valve opens before the onset of ventricular contraction, permitting presystolic flow and a presystolic murmur (see Fig. 10.5).78,80,86 Presystolic murmurs are occasionally generated by prolonged vibrations of a fourth heart sound,78 and soft diastolic murmurs have been attributed to low-pressure pulmonary regurgitation (see Figs. 10.2B, 10.5, and 10.20B).80,86 Dysplastic or calcific pulmonary valves88 are rarely incompetent.

paragraphs.text: Systolic murmurs of pulmonary artery stenosis are crescendodecrescendo (see Figs. 10.21 and 10.22) with delayed onset because of their relatively distal origins (see Fig. 10.22). Stenoses originating at or near the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk generate murmurs that occasionally reach grade 4/6 in the second left intercostal space, but as a rule, the central precordial murmur is grade 3/6 and the peripheral murmurs are softer. When the intensities of precordial and nonprecordial murmurs are equal, it can be assumed that the widespread nonprecordial murmurs originate peripherally. Intrapulmonary phonocardiograms confirm that systolic murmurs originate distal to stenoses in the pulmonary trunk and proximal pulmonary arterial branches (see Figs. 10.21 through 10.23) Peripheral pulmonary systolic murmurs are overlooked because of their low intensity and because auscultation is not routinely conducted at nonprecordial sites. The difficulty is compounded in infants because of rapid respiratory rates and because the frequency composition of breath sounds is close to the frequency of composition of peripheral pulmonary systolic murmurs. The diaphragm of the stethoscope should be applied during held respiration with the patient supine, prone, and sitting comfortably.
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: Continuous murmurs imply continuous gradients across the stenotic sites, but recordings of pressure pulses proximal and distal to the zones of stenosis show that systolic gradients seldom continue into diastole.90 The central pulmonary arterial pulse is characterized by an elevated systolic pressure and a rapid fall to diastolic levels that are normal or nearly so (see Figs. 10.22 and 10.10). Gradients are confined to systolic, so the accompanying murmur is confined to systole (see Figs. 10.22 and 10.10).90 Why,

paragraphs.text: then, do continuous murmurs occur at all? It has been postulated that systolic expansion of the high-pressure pulmonary trunk proximal to the stenosis sets the stage for brisk diastolic flow across the distal segments as the expanded proximal segments recoil.90 Modest diastolic flow following a large systolic gradient explains the occasional occurrence of a soft, low-frequency diastolic murmur that precedes a prominent systolic murmur. Pulmonary artery stenosis may also give rise to increased flow through bronchial arterial collaterals.91 Angiographically demonstrated bronchial collaterals are believed to be responsible for continuous murmurs.92
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: Splitting of the second heart sound and the intensity of the pulmonary component are important signs in the auscultatory characterization of obstruction to right ventricular outflow. In typical mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis, the intensity of the pulmonary component varies from normal to inaudible as severity increases (see Figs. 10.15 through 10.20). However, timing is more important than intensity in assessing severity.80,85 The more severe the stenosis, the longer the duration of right ventricular ejection, the later the timing of pulmonary valve closure, and the wider the split (see Fig. 10.15). paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: In pulmonary artery stenosis, factors that influence the behavior of the second heart sound differ from those that influence the second sound in valvular or subvalvular stenosis.89 Stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches is unique among causes of pulmonary hypertension because it elevates systolic but not diastolic pressure in the pulmonary trunk. Accordingly, the valve closes at a normal or near-normal pressure, so the intensity of the pulmonary component of the second sound is normal (Figs. 10.24 and 10.25; see also Fig. 10.10).24,89,96 The abruptness with which the leaflets seat affects the intensity of the pulmonary component of the second heart sound. The cusps might bulge abruptly toward the right ventricle during isometric relaxation, suddenly increasing the volume capacity of the pulmonary trunk. paragraphs.text: component varies inversely with the degree of stenosis. The timing of pulmonary valve closure cannot be judged by criteria that apply to valvular or fixed subvalvular pulmonary stenosis, both of which prolong right ventricular ejection. Potential prolongation of right ventricular ejection in pulmonary artery stenosis is countered by the rapidity with which the pulmonary artery pressure falls from its systolic peak (see Fig. 10.22). The second heart sound is therefore normally split even in the presence of appreciable obstruction;22 the degree of splitting varies appropriately with respiration (see Figs. 10.24 and 10.25).89
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: Abrahams and Wood drew attention to the significance of fourth heart sounds in pulmonary stenosis,13 reasoning that “strong right atrial contraction in presystole helps the hypertrophied right ventricle generate a high systolic pressure.” This was considered “an example of Starling’s law of the heart, strong atrial systole augmenting late diastolic distention of the right ventricle so that the chamber contracts more forcibly.” Presystolic distension of the right ventricle and fourth heart sounds are features of severe pulmonary stenosis because these physiologic conditions prevail when obstruction to right ventricular outflow is severe (Fig. 10.26; see also Figs. 10.12B and 10.15).80
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: As severity increases, P waves become tall and peaked (Fig. 10.27).97 Giant P waves occasionally appear especially in lead 2 (Fig. 10.28). The P wave in lead V1 may be entirely negative because the P terminal force is written by a dilated right atrium (see Fig. 10.28).98 Pulmonary regurgitation (PR) interval prolongation has been attributed to an increase in right atrial size that prolongs the transit time from the sinus node to the atrioventricular node (Fig. 10.29).30 Right axis deviation tends to vary with right ventricular systolic pressure (Fig. 10.30; see also Figs. 10.27 through 10.29).59 Superior orientation of the QRS axis occurs in infants with pulmonary artery stenosis and the rubella syndrome.99

paragraphs.text: The configuration of the QRS in lead V1 varies (see Fig. 10.31). In mild pulmonary stenosis, an rSr9 is difficult to distinguish from normal.91,101,102 With greater degrees of stenosis, the terminal R wave becomes taller, writing an rsR pattern (see Fig. 10.30),91 or a small r wave appears as a notch on the upstroke of a tall R prime (see Figs. 10.30 and 10.31). The neonate with pinpoint pulmonary stenosis and a small right ventricular cavity has an electrocardiogram that resembles pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum, namely, a normal QRS axis and adult progression in precordial leads (Fig. 10.32).103 In subinfundibular pulmonary stenosis (double-chambered right ventricle), a smaller portion of the right ventricle is in the

paragraphs.text: In normal neonates, upright right precordial T waves become inverted by 4 days of age. In infants and children with mild pulmonary stenosis, upright right precordial T waves may persist as the only electrocardiographic sign of elevated right ventricular systolic pressure (Fig. 10.33).104 In severe pulmonary stenosis, the T wave direction shifts leftward, superiorly, and posteriorly as the QRS axis shifts to the right and anteriorly. The QRS-T angle widens, so inverted T waves appear in leads 2, 3, aVF, and in right
paragraphs.heading: The Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: precordial leads (see Figs. 10.27 and 10.28). Deeply inverted T waves that cove upward on their descending limbs and are accompanied by ST segment depressions extending beyond lead V2 are features of severe pulmonary stenosis (see Figs. 10.27 and 10.28).
paragraphs.heading: The Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome with dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis has an electrocardiogram that differs from the patterns just described. Axis deviation may be extreme,19,105 the QRS tends to be splintered and prolonged, and a QS pattern appears in inferior and left precordial leads.15 However, the pattern of left axis deviation, abnormal R/S ratio over the left precordium with abnormal Q waves is related to the syndrome per se and not to a specific accompanying cardiac defect.106
paragraphs.heading: The Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary vascularity remains normal even in severe pulmonary stenosis until the right ventricle fails and blood flow to the lungs declines (Fig. 10.34). Flow to the right lung is occasionally less than flow to the left lung (unequal distribution).107 Radiologic signs of pulmonary artery stenosis include zones of segmental hypovascularity that correspond to locations of the arterial obstructions and areas of fusiform intrapulmonary dilation beyond the zones of stenosis (Fig. 10.35; see also Figs. 10.8 and 10.9B).24
paragraphs.heading: The X-Ray

paragraphs.text: A conspicuous increase in right atrial and right ventricular size are radiologic signs of severity, especially when the enlargement appears at an early age (see Fig. 10.34). The dilated right ventricle is rounded rather than boot-shaped, and its apex lies above the left hemidiaphragm (see Fig. 10.34). The aortic arch is left-sided, with rare exception (see Fig. 10.7).108 In Noonan syndrome, in contrast to Turner syndrome, ascending aortic dilatation is rare (see Chapter 7).109

paragraphs.heading: The X-Ray

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary stenosis was one of the first lesions where echocardiography made substantial early contributions to anatomic diagnosis and management.114 Color flow imaging in typical mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis discloses a high-velocity jet directed toward the left pulmonary artery (see Fig. 10.5).114 Continuous-wave Doppler establishes the velocity across the stenotic pulmonary valve from which the peak instantaneous gradient can be estimated (see Fig. 10.5).114
paragraphs.heading: The Echocardiogram

paragraphs.text: During right ventricular systole, the mobile pulmonary valve domes briskly cephalad as a single unit. A bicuspid pulmonary valve can occasionally be identified.115 In severe pulmonary stenosis, the increased force of right atrial contraction is transmitted into the right ventricle onto the undersurface of the mobile pulmonary valve which opens in presystole, generating a Doppler signal (see Fig. 10.5) (see earlier). Secondary hypertrophic subpulmonary stenosis is recognized as an envelope within the major continuous-wave Doppler signal (see Fig. 10.5). Mild pulmonary regurgitation is occasionally detected in the presence of pulmonary valve stenosis.

paragraphs.heading: The Echocardiogram

paragraphs.text: Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis is imaged as thickened immobile leaflets. The pulmonary trunk is not significantly dilated. Stenosis of the ostium of the infundibulum and subinfundibular stenosis (double-chambered right ventricle) can be identified and physiologically assessed. Pulmonary artery stenosis is accompanied by a normal-sized pulmonary trunk and small proximal pulmonary arteries. Doppler interrogation records the velocities across the sites of branch stenosis, and distinguishes congenital pulmonary artery
paragraphs.heading: The Echocardiogram

paragraphs.text: stenosis from the normal neonatal physiologic drop in systolic pressure between the pulmonary trunk and its proximal branches.26
paragraphs.heading: The Echocardiogram

paragraphs.text: The murmur of mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis dates from birth. The physical appearance in infancy is sometimes represented by round bloated facies and well-developed fat pads. The jugular venous A wave is prominent, even giant; the right ventricular impulse is as high as the third left intercostal space. Auscultation detects a pulmonary ejection sound, a midsystolic systolic murmur that radiates upward and to the left, and a delayed soft pulmonary component of the second heart sound. A thrill is maximum in the second left intercostal space. The

paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis is a feature of Noonan syndrome that is recognized by a distinctive phenotype. Echocardiography identifies the thickened dysplastic cusps that exhibit little or no motion. Because of the limited mobility of the thickened dysplastic valve, a pulmonary ejection sound and the pulmonary component of the second heart sound are absent.

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary artery stenosis is accompanied by a murmur that may not be identified at birth. The history may disclose familial recurrence and hemoptysis from rupture of thin-walled intrapulmonary aneurysms distal to the sites of stenoses. The physical appearance of the rubella syndrome or Williams syndrome constitutes important evidence. A pulmonary ejection sound is absent, there is normal intensity and splitting of the second heart sound, and widespread systolic murmurs are heard in the axillae and back. paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: The morphology of the congenitally malformed valve is variable.116–118 One, two, or three cusps may undergo faulty development,119,120 all three cusps may be rudimentary,119 one cusp may be absent121 and the other two rudimentary,118 very rarely the pulmonary cusps are dysplastic,122 or there may be no valve tissue at all—congenital absence of the pulmonary valve123,124 as reported by Chevers in 1846.125 The anomaly seldom occurs in isolation,126–130 but instead coexists with Fallot’s tetralogy131 (see Chapter 15) and sporadically with other malformations.118,132,133
paragraphs.heading: PULMONARY REGURGITATION Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: A bicuspid pulmonary valve is rare as an isolated anomaly and is only occasionally incompetent. A quadricuspid pulmonary valve typically occurs with truncus arteriosus (see Chapter 25) and only rarely in isolation.134,135 If the four cusps are equal, the quadricuspid valve functions normally, but if there is cuspal inequality or a supernumerary cusp, the valve is rendered incompetent, especially if the pulmonary artery pressure is elevated.134
paragraphs.heading: PULMONARY REGURGITATION Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: Significance of the diagnosis of pulmonary valve regurgitation must take into account the relatively high incidence of trivial to mild pulmonary regurgitation identified incidentally by color flow imaging and Doppler interrogation in individuals whose hearts are structurally normal.136,137 Prevalence from birth to age 14 years is nil under 1 year of age, with a peak incidence of 42% between 6 and 11 years of age.136
paragraphs.heading: Physiologic Consequences

paragraphs.text: The mature right ventricle is a low-pressure low-resistance pump that readily adapts to augmented volume, although the degree and duration of regurgitant flow are important determinants of this response.117 The physiologic consequences of pulmonary regurgitation are especially dramatic in utero because systemic pressure in the pulmonary trunk augments regurgitant flow, more so if there is agenesis of the fetal ductus.119,129 Acquired elevation of pulmonary arterial pressure in adults with bronchopulmonary disease or left ventricular failure are analogous but less dramatic.138
paragraphs.heading: Physiologic Consequences

paragraphs.text: Isolated congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation usually comes to light because of a murmur or because of a dilated pulmonary arterial trunk in a routine chest x-ray. The diagnosis tends to be delayed, however, because the murmur is not detected at birth,119 and routine chest x-rays are seldom done before adulthood. Sex distribution is about equal.139
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Clinical manifestations of isolated congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation fall into three categories. The first and largest category consists of asymptomatic children, adolescents, and young adults116,139 who tolerate the anomaly through middle age,140 and occasionally into the sixth or even eighth decade.141 Isolated congenital absence of the pulmonary valve has been reported at age 69 years142 and 73 years.128
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: The second and much smaller category consists of adults in whom right ventricular failure occurs after decades of stability.138,139 Severe pulmonary valve regurgitation per se can cause the right ventricle to fail,143 but moderate regurgitation produces little or no ill effect until the degree of regurgitant flow is increased by adult-acquired elevation in pulmonary artery pressure associated with bronchopulmonary disease143 or left ventricular failure.138
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Infective endocarditis is a low probability cause of increased regurgitation.
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: A third and rare category of congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation occurs in the fetus129 or neonate119,139 when elevated pulmonary arterial pressure augments the volume of regurgitant flow across a congenitally malformed or absent pulmonary valve.129,139 In utero patency of the ductus is desirable because ductal agenesis increases resistance to right ventricular discharge and increases regurgitant flow. The converse is the case with ductal patency after birth which adds to the burden of the right ventricle by allowing diastolic flow to proceed from the aorta through the ductus into the pulmonary artery and across the incompetent pulmonary valve into the right ventricle.127,129,139,144
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Physical appearance and the arterial pulse are normal. The A wave, V wave, and mean jugular venous pressure rise with the advent of right ventricular failure.
paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance, the Arterial Pulse, and the Jugular Venous Pulse

paragraphs.text: When pulmonary regurgitation is mild to moderate, the right ventricular impulse is gentle and is detected only in the subxiphoid area during held inspiration. Severe regurgitation that accompanies congenital absence of the pulmonary valve generates a hyperdynamic impulse at the left sternal border and subxiphoid area, in addition to an impulse in the second left intercostal space caused by systolic expansion of the dilated pulmonary trunk (Fig. 10.41).139,141
paragraphs.heading: Precordial Movement and Palpation

paragraphs.text: A normal first heart sound is occasionally followed by an ejection sound into the dilated pulmonary trunk. The pulmonary component of the second heart sound is absent when the leaflets are absent or rudimentary139,145 and soft when the cusps are present but defective, although audibility per se indicates the presence of valve tissue.146 The split tends to be wide because of a delay in the pulmonary component caused by increased capacitance of the pulmonary vascular bed and slow elastic recoil.94,146,147 The occasional occurrence of complete right bundle branch block also delays the pulmonary component of the second sound (Fig. 10.42). Inspiration increases the degree of splitting unless the right ventricle has failed.146 Narrow splitting sometimes occurs because rapid right ventricular ejection coupled with brisk decline in the descending limb of the pulmonary artery pressure pulse cancels a potential delay in pulmonary valve closure.
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: The hallmark of congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation is the distinctive diastolic murmur.
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: The murmur of low-pressure, low-velocity regurgitant flow is maximum in the second or third left intercostal space, medium to low pitched, crescendo decrescendo, delayed in onset, and short in duration, ending well before the subsequent first heart sound (Fig. 10.43; see also Fig. 10.42).139,140,143,148 The murmur begins immediately after the right ventricular and pulmonary arterial pressure pulses diverge in early diastole and is the loudest at the timing of an early diastolic dip when the diastolic gradient is maximum (Fig. 10.44A).143,148 If the pulmonary component of the second heart sound is soft or absent, a silent interval exists between the aortic component and the onset of the diastolic murmur (see Fig. 10.43).148 Equilibration of pulmonary arterial and right ventricular pressures in latter diastole reduces or eliminates the regurgitant gradient and eliminates the murmur (Figs. 10.45 and 10.46; see also Fig. 10.44A).148 The normally low diastolic

Accordingly, the low to medium-frequency diastolic murmur ends well before the subsequent first heart sound (see Fig. 10.44A). Mild congenital pulmonary regurgitation permits the diastolic pressure in the pulmonary trunk to remain higher than the diastolic pressure in the right ventricle, so the low- to medium-frequency murmur extends throughout diastole (see Fig. 10.46).
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: The intensity of the diastolic murmur varies from grade 1 to 3/6, but it is exceptionally loud and rough enough to generate a thrill.140,141 During inspiration, the early diastolic dip in the right ventricular pressure pulse falls more rapidly than the diastolic pressure in the pulmonary trunk, so the regurgitant gradient transiently increases and the murmur becomes correspondingly louder.129
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: A midsystolic murmur with congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation is due to rapid ejection of an increased right ventricular stroke volume into a dilated pulmonary trunk (see Fig. 10.42).139 The systolic murmur is short and crescendo-decrescendo, ending well before both components of the second heart sound (see Fig. 10.42). Rarely, a low-frequency presystolic murmur assigned to vibrations of the tricuspid valve is believed to represent a rightsided Austin Flint.139
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: exceptional even with congenital absence of the pulmonary valve.142 The most common change in the QRS reflects the pattern of volume overload of the right ventricle and is represented by terminal r waves in leads V1 and aVR and S waves in leads 1 and V5–6 (Fig. 10.47).95,139,142 Right bundle branch block is uncommon (see Fig. 10.42).116,142
paragraphs.heading: The Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: Dilatation of the pulmonary trunk is the most prominent and consistent feature of the x-ray (see Fig. 10.41).95,140,141 The dilation has been ascribed to coexisting medial abnormalities16 and varies considerably in size, sometimes reaching aneurysmal proportions (see Fig. 10.41).123 Vigorous pulsations of the pulmonary trunk and its proximal branches are seen with fluoroscopy139,140 and with real time echocardiography (see next section). Occasionally, the chest x-ray fortuitously records striking intermittent changes in the size of the dilated pulmonary trunk (see Fig. 10.41).141 Right ventricular enlargement corresponds to the degree of volume overload.
paragraphs.heading: The X-Ray

paragraphs.text: Color flow imaging and Doppler interrogation establish the diagnosis of congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation and establish the depth, width, duration, and peak velocity of the diastolic jet (Fig. 10.48) that differs from pulmonary hypertensive pulmonary regurgitation (Figs. 10.49 and 10.50). Mild pulmonary regurgitation detected in normal subjects is not accompanied by a diastolic murmur.136,137
paragraphs.heading: The Echocardiogram

paragraphs.text: Echocardiography defines the size of the pulmonary trunk and its proximal branches and the vigor of pulsations in response to rapid ejection of the regurgitant volume. The physiologic consequences of congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation are reflected in the size and contractility of the right ventricle and in paradoxical motion of the ventricular septum.
paragraphs.heading: The Echocardiogram

paragraphs.text: Congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation comes to light in healthy asymptomatic individuals who exhibit dilation of the pulmonary trunk in a routine chest x-ray, or in whom diastolic/ systolic murmurs are discovered on routine physical examination.

paragraphs.text: An exception is the neonate with severe isolated congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation or complete absence of the pulmonary valve. Precordial palpation detects a right ventricular impulse that corresponds to the degree of regurgitation. Systolic expansion of the pulmonary trunk imparts an impulse in the second left intercostal space. Auscultation reveals a distinctive diastolic murmur that is maximum in the second or third left interspace, low to medium frequency, crescendodecrescendo, delayed in onset, short in duration, and occasionally louder during inspiration. A pulmonary midsystolic murmur is usually present. The second heart sound is normal or widely split, the pulmonary component is soft or inaudible, and the split tends to be persistent but not fixed. The electrocardiogram is either normal or exhibits signs of volume overload of the right ventricle with an rSr prime in lead V1. The x-ray shows dilation of the pulmonary trunk that is occasionally aneurysmal together with dilatation of the right ventricle. Color flow imaging and Doppler interrogation establish the presence and degree of pulmonary regurgitation and its physiologic consequences.

figures.caption: Fig. 10.1 ​(A and B) Angiocardiograms with contrast material injected into the right ventricle of a 47-year-old female with pulmonary valve stenosis (gradient 106 mm Hg). (A) Arrow points to the level of the stenotic pulmonary valve. The dilated pulmonary trunk (PT) continues as a dilated left branch (LPA). (B) Lateral projection. The stenotic pulmonary valve is mobile and domed (arrow), and the PT is conspicuously dilated. There is an hourglass narrowing of the ostium of the infundibulum. (C and D) Angiocardiograms with contrast material injected into the right ventricle (RV) of a 10-month-old female with pinpoint pulmonary valve stenosis. (C) A wisp of contrast crosses the valve (arrows), and faintly visualizes the dilated PT. (D) The mobile stenotic valve is dome-shaped (arrow), and the PT is conspicuously dilated.

figures.caption: Fig. 10.5 ​Continuous-wave Doppler from a 32-year-old male with severe mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis (PS) and secondary hypertrophic subpulmonary stenosis (compare to Fig. 10.4). The velocity across the stenotic pulmonary valve was 5.4 cm, indicating a peak instantaneous gradient of 117 mm Hg. The asymmetric profile within the envelope of the continuous-wave Doppler signal represents the gradient across the zone of secondary hypertrophic subpulmonary stenosis (Sub PS). Pulmonary regurgitation was mild. The small presystolic Doppler signal (upper left) was caused by opening the mobile pulmonary valve by powerful right atrial contraction that was transmitted into the right ventricle and onto the undersurface of the pulmonary valve.

10 10 Congenital Pulmonary Stenosis and Regurgitation

### HISTORICAL NOTES

Dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis was described in 1761 by John Baptist Morgagni.1 In 1941, McAlister Gregg, an Australian ophthalmologist, described a relationship between maternal rubella and congenital abnormalities in offspring.2 What came to be known as the rubella syndrome consists of stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches with patent ductus arteriosus.3,4 Subinfundibular stenosis or double-chambered right ventricle was described by Thomas Peacock who recognized the murmur in 1858.5 Obstructing muscle bundles within the right ventricular cavity were the subject of Sir Arthur Keith’s Hunterian lecture in 1909.6 Pulmonary artery stenosis (supravalvular) was described by Oppenheimer in 1938.7

William Osler described pulmonary regurgitation in The Principles and Practice of Medicine (1892).8 This rare affection is occasionally due to a congenital malformation, particularly fusion of the two segments ... The condition is extremely rare and of little practical significance. The distinctive diastolic murmur of low-pressure pulmonary regurgitation was characterized in 1910,9 and in 1936, isolated congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation was reported with a review of the literature.10 Maude Abbott’s necropsy study of 1000 cases of congenital heart disease included two examples of isolated congenital pulmonary valve regurgitation.11 In 1955, the first clinical diagnosis was made in an asymptomatic 24-year-old medical student.12

This chapter is concerned with isolated obstruction of the pulmonary valve or right ventricular outflow tract and pulmonary valve regurgitation as an isolated congenital malformation. It does not include pulmonary stenosis that occurs in conjunction with complex congenital heart disease or pulmonary regurgitation associated with pulmonary hypertension.

### PULMONARY STENOSIS Incidence and Prevalence

Typical mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis is relatively common with a prevalence as high as 10% of cases of congenital heart disease.13,14 Sex distribution is equal or with female prevalence.14 This is also the case in dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis.15

### Anatomic Considerations

Congenital obstruction to right ventricular outflow in hearts with two non-inverted ventricles originates in, below or above the pulmonary valve. Three morphologic types of pulmonary stenosis involve the pulmonary valve: (1) typical mobile dome-shaped, (2) dysplastic, and (3) bicuspid. Dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis is characterized by a thin mobile valve mechanism with a narrow central opening at its apex (Fig. 10.1). Three rudimentary raphes extend from the central opening to the wall of the pulmonary artery, but separate leaflets and separate commissures cannot be identified. Pinpoint dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis in neonates is sometimes referred to as functional pulmonary atresia (see Fig. 10.1, lower, A and B). The pulmonary trunk is consistently dilated because an inherent medial abnormality16 is coupled

with the mobile dome-shaped valve, but not with its functional state (see Fig. 10.1). The jet from the stenotic valve breaks up upon striking the apex of the pulmonary trunk. The pressure component of total energy increases with a proportionate increase pressure in the left branch (Fig. 10.2A).17 The physics of jet dispersion is believed to account for the larger size of the left branch. Calcification of a dome-shaped stenotic pulmonary valve is exceptional and is reserved for older patients.18 Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis is much less common and is characterized by myomatous thickening of three separate but poorly mobile leaflets without commissural fusion (Fig. 10.3 and Box 10.1).19,20 Bicuspid pulmonary valve stenosis is a feature of Fallot’s tetralogy (see Chapter 13). Isolated bicuspid pulmonary valves are rare and are of little or no functional significance.

Subvalvular pulmonary stenosis can be infundibular or subinfundibular. The infundibular variety is caused by anterior and rightward deviation (malalignment) of the infundibular septum and is dealt with in Chapter 13. Secondary hypertrophic infundibular pulmonary stenosis accompanies—is secondary to—severe pulmonary valve stenosis (Figs. 10.4 and 10.5). Stenosis of the ostium of the infundibulum is a rare form of fixed obstruction to right ventricular outflow (Figs. 10.6 and 10.7). Subinfundibular stenosis or double-chambered right ventricle is a rare form of congenital obstruction to right ventricular outflow. Obstructing muscle bundles within the right ventricular cavity result in a double-chambered right ventricle; the right ventricle is hence divided into a high-pressure inlet portion and a low-pressure outlet portion by normal or anomalous muscle bundles21,22 or by apical trabecular muscle sequestered from the rest of the right ventricle.23 The degree of obstruction varies from nil to severe to virtually complete.22 Double-chambered right ventricle usually coexists with a ventricular septal defect.21,22

Pulmonary artery stenosis (supravalvular) is caused by narrowing of the pulmonary trunk, its bifurcation, or its primary or intrapulmonary branches (Figs. 10.8 and 10.9).24 Stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches usually occurs as an isolated malformation24 and can be unilateral or bilateral, single or multiple, and segmental or tubular (see Figs. 10.8 and 10.9).24 Intrapulmonary arteries distal to the stenoses tend to be dilated (see Figs. 10.8 and 10.9). Rarely, a membranous form of obstruction occurs immediately above the valve.24

Neonates, especially premature, normally exhibit a disparity in size between the pulmonary trunk and its proximal branches. Angulations at the origins of the branches cause a drop in systolic pressure in the absence of morphologic pulmonary artery stenosis (see Chapter 2 and Fig. 2.4).25,26 The small pulmonary trunk and small proximal branches in Fallot’s tetralogy are discussed in Chapter 15. In Williams syndrome, bilateral stenosis of pulmonary artery branches is associated with supravalvular aortic stenosis (see Chapter 7).27 Experimental constriction of the pulmonary trunk in fetal lambs results in thin-walled intrapulmonary resistance vessels.28

### Physiologic Consequences

The physiological consequences of pulmonary stenosis result from increased resistance to right ventricular discharge. Systolic pressure is elevated proximal to the obstruction and is normal or reduced distally. Pulmonary artery stenosis causes an increase in systolic pressure in the pulmonary trunk which is proximal to the obstruction (Fig. 10.10). ### The History

Patients with isolated pulmonary stenosis tend to have a favorable long-term prognosis35 with little progression of disease in

10

PT

those with mild valvar pulmonary stenosis.36 Even so, great strides have been made in diagnostic capabilities and therapeutic options for patients with obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract further optimizing outcomes.37,38

Familial recurrence of isolated pulmonary valve stenosis is uncommon if not rare (Fig. 10.11).39–42 In dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis, the converse is the case.19 Some family members have a dysplastic valve, while others have a mobile dome-shaped valve.19 Familial Noonan syndrome frequently occurs with dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis and has appeared in three generations.43,44 Successful pregnancy is possible in females with Noonan syndrome.45 Familial pulmonary artery stenosis occurs as an isolated anomaly or with coexisting supravalvular aortic stenosis. Members of the same family may have either or both anomalies.

Genetic anomalies have been associated with pulmonary stenosis with and without Noonan syndrome. Cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome occurs sporadically with multiple congenital anomalies where pulmonary stenosis is more common in individuals with a BRAF mutation.46 PTPN11 mutations cause LEOPARD syndrome and Noonan syndrome, both of which are part of a family of autosomal dominant syndromes termed “RASopathies,” which are developmental diseases caused by mutations in genes encoding for signal transducers of the RAS-MAPK cascade.47,48 Cardiac defects occur in 80% of these with worst outcomes described in those with Noonan syndrome and pulmonary stenosis who carry the PTPN11 mutations.48

Normal birth weights and normal growth and development are characteristic of mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis. However, in Noonan syndrome with dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis, growth and development are poor.15,19,49 Pulmonary artery stenosis is associated with low birth weights and retarded physical and mental development in the rubella syndrome and in Williams syndrome (see Chapter 7).3,50

Neonates with pinpoint pulmonary valve stenosis experience rapidly progressive cardiac failure. However, the majority of patients with mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis experience little or no difficulty in infancy and childhood.36 In a review of 69 cases, the average age at death was 26 years, seven patients survived to age 50 years, and three survived to 70 and 75 years. In 21 adults, the average follow-up was 50 years.51 There are examples of survival into the sixth, seventh, and eighth decade,52–56 with one patient reaching 78 years.52 Longevity depends on three variables: (1) the initial severity of stenosis, (2) whether a given

The normal pulmonary valve orifice increases linearly with age and body surface area.58 The orifice of a stenotic mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve increases with age, but not necessarily at the rate of somatic growth.36,58–60 Mild pulmonary valve stenosis in infancy usually remains mild,61 but moderate to severe pulmonary stenosis tends to progress.54 Stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches is not progressive. Fibrous thickening and occasionally calcification are responsible for increasing the degree of stenosis in older adults.

Equivalent degrees of pulmonary stenosis may handicap one patient in childhood but leave another relatively free of symptoms in adulthood. It is not surprising that mild pulmonary stenosis is asymptomatic, but it is surprising that an appreciable number of patients with moderate to severe pulmonary stenosis claim to be virtually asymptomatic. Patients with right ventricular systolic pressures between 50 and 100 mm Hg include a New Zealand long-distance swimmer, a long-distance runner, and an English hockey captain.62 My patients include a 17-yearold boy who played baseball despite a right ventricular systolic pressure of nearly 200 mm Hg, a 32-year-old male who had run the quarter mile in high school despite a right ventricular systolic pressure of 75 mm Hg, and a female with a right ventricular pressure of nearly 200 mm Hg who worked full-time and had recurrent ascites for 7 years before death at age 60 years. Dyspnea and fatigue are mild as long as the right ventricle maintains a normal stroke volume at rest and augments its stroke volume with exercise.32,57 However, relatively asymptomatic patients can deteriorate rapidly. Cardiac output is inadequate even at rest when the hemodynamic burden imposed on the right ventricle leads to right ventricular failure, the commonest cause of death.53

Giddiness and light-headedness with effort prefigure syncope.62 Children as well as adults occasionally experience the chest pain of right ventricular myocardial ischemia.56,63 A 3-year-old with severe pulmonary artery stenosis died during an episode of chest pain and at necropsy had infarction of the right ventricular free wall and interventricular septum.63 Sudden death has been associated with right ventricular infarction and an abnormal right coronary artery.64 Dilated thin-walled intrapulmonary artery aneurysms distal to the stenoses of pulmonary artery branches (see Fig. 10.9B) are sources of hemoptyses that can be intermittent and mild or recurrent and brisk.24

### Physical Appearance

Six physical appearances are relevant in patients with congenital pulmonary stenosis: (1) the round bloated facies in infants with mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis, (2) Noonan syndrome, (3) the rubella syndrome, (4) Williams syndrome, (5) Alagille syndrome, and (6) the Cornelia de Lange syndrome.

Infants with mobile dome-shaped pulmonary valve stenosis occasionally have chubby round bloated facies with highly colored cheeks (Fig. 10.13A) and well-developed fat deposits.62 The digits may be erythematous or frankly red in response to a small or intermittent right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale. Noonan syndrome45,65,66 (see Fig. 10.13C) is characterized by short stature, webbed neck, pterygium colli, ptosis, hypertelorism, lymphedema, low-set ears, low anterior and posterior hairlines, flat or shield chest, pectus excavatum or carinatum, hyperelastic skin, inguinal hernia, nevi, dystrophic nails, micrognathia, hypospadias, and small undescended or cryptorchid testes,44,65 foramen ovale (see Chapter 12).

About one-third of Noonan patients are intellectually disabled, and approximately two-thirds have congenital heart disease, especially dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis (60%) or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (20%).65,67,68 Mild pulmonary stenosis in patients with Noonan syndrome is typically nonprogressive.69 Malignant tumor development is a complication encountered in other RASopathies, though the neoplastic risks and incidence of malignant tumors are less clearly defined in Noonan syndrome and related disorders of the Noonan spectrum.70

The rubella syndrome is characterized by cataracts, retinopathy, deafness, hypotonia, dermatoglyphic abnormalities, and intellectual disability.71 Height and weight are usually normal for age despite intrauterine growth retardation. Stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches and patent ductus arteriosus (see Chapter 17) are the most frequent types of coexisting congenital heart disease.71

Williams syndrome includes a small chin, large mouth, patulous lips, blunt upturned nose, wide-set eyes, broad forehead, baggy cheeks, and malformed teeth (see Chapter 7). The most frequent coexisting congenital heart disease is pulmonary artery stenosis with supravalvular aortic stenosis (see Chapter 7).

Alagille syndrome, also called arteriohepatic dysplasia or the Alagille-Watson syndrome, is an autosomal dominant disorder with abnormalities of liver, eyes, kidneys, and skeleton.72,73 Facial appearance is characterized by a prominent overhanging forehead, deep-set eyes, and a small pointed chin (see Fig. 10.13B).72–74 The most frequent coexisting congenital heart disease is stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches.73

Cornelia de Lange syndrome expresses itself as low birth weight; slow growth; small stature; microcephaly; thin eyebrows that meet at midline; long eyelashes; short upturned nose; thin, downturned lips; hirsutism; small hands and feet; in-curved fifth fingers; cleft palate; and missing limbs or portions of limbs. The incidence of pulmonary valve stenosis is reportedly 39%.75

Pulmonary stenosis also occurs in the LEOPARD syndrome that is characterized by multiple lentigines and café-au-lait spots.76

### The Arterial Pulse

When severe pulmonary stenosis is accompanied by right ventricular failure, especially with coexisting left ventricular dysfunction, the arterial pulse is reduced. Asymmetry of right and left brachial and carotid arterial pulses (right greater than left) is a feature of supravalvular aortic stenosis that may accompany stenosis of the pulmonary artery and its branches (see Chapter 7).

### The Jugular Venous Pulse

The jugular venous A wave is distinctive, increasing progressively as the stenosis increases (Fig. 10.14; see also Fig. 10.12A), culminating in a giant A wave that leaps to the eye, towering above and dwarfing the other waves of the venous pulse.13 Powerful right atrial contraction generates a giant A wave via the superior vena cava and a presystolic liver pulse via the inferior cava. With the advent of right ventricular failure and tricuspid regurgitation, the large A wave is accompanied by an increase in the V wave. The liver then manifests presystolic and systolic pulsations.

### Precordial Movement and Palpation

The thrill associated with pulmonary valve stenosis is maximum in the second left intercostal space with radiation upward and to the left because the intrapulmonary jet is directed upward and toward the left pulmonary artery (see Fig. 10.2A).17 When secondary hypertrophic subpulmonary stenosis coexists, the thrill is maximum in the third or fourth left intercostal space (see Fig. 10.4).

Palpation of the right ventricular impulse is best achieved by applying the fingertips between the ribs along the left sternal edge during full held exhalation or when a single fingertip is applied against the diaphragm in the subxiphoid area.77,78 The subxiphoid technique is especially useful in infants because rapid respiratory excursions interfere with parasternal palpation. In severe pulmonary valve stenosis, the right ventricular impulse is forceful and sustained and is detected up to and including the third intercostal space.77–79 Infundibular pulmonary stenosis relegates the high-pressure zone to the inflow portion of the right

Subinfundibular stenosis is accompanied by a deceptively unimpressive right ventricular impulse confined to the fifth interspace or subxiphoid area. The pulmonary trunk is necessarily distal to the stenosis and cannot be palpated despite conspicuous dilatation.

A presystolic impulse along the lower-left sternal border and in the subxiphoid area (see Fig. 10.12B) indicates presystolic distention of the right ventricle in response to the increased force of right atrial contraction that is also responsible for the large jugular venous A wave (see Fig. 10.12A). A prominent pulmonary ejection sound is occasionally palpable in the second left intercostal space during held exhalation.

sound can also originate in a functionally normal bicuspid pulmonary valve.81 The sound is recognized by its high-pitched clicking quality, by its maximum intensity in the second left intercostal space and by its distinctive selective decrease during inspiration (Figs. 10.16 through 10.18).78,82,83 The inspiratory decrease is related to the reduced cephalad movement available to the mobile valve as the right ventricle contracts.82 The inspiratory increase in right atrial contractile force is transmitted into the right ventricle and onto the undersurface of the mobile pulmonary valve that moves into a relatively cephalad position.84 Additional cephalad movement is necessarily reduced, so the ejection sound is reduced or vanishes altogether.82 Conversely, the right atrial contractile force decreases during expiration, leaving the mobile pulmonary valve in a slack position, so right ventricular contraction induces maximum cephalad movement and maximum intensity of the ejection sound.82

The interval between the first heart sound and the ejection sound varies inversely with the degree of stenosis (see Fig. 10.15).80,85 As severity increases, the velocity of right ventricular contraction increases, the pulmonary valve opens earlier, and the ejection sound occurs earlier and merges with the first heart sound (see Fig. 10.15) but retains its distinctive respiratory variation that distinguishes it from a loud first heart sound.85,86 Accordingly, a pulmonary ejection sound that occurs at a welldefined interval after the first heart sound is a sign of mild pulmonary valve stenosis, and an ejection sound that merges with the first heart sound is a sign of severe pulmonary stenosis. Fibrosis and calcification in older patients impair mobility, so the ejection sound decreases or disappears altogether.

The maximum precordial site is the second left intercostal space (see Figs. 10.16 through 10.18) that topographically overlies the pulmonary trunk and coincides with the location of the murmur recorded by intracardiac phonocardiography (see Fig. 10.16B).78 Prominence of the murmur in the third left intercostal space occurs with secondary hypertrophic subpulmonary stenosis (Fig. 10.19B; see also Fig 10.4). The murmur radiates upward and to the left (see Fig. 10.17) because the intrapulmonary jet is directed upward and to the left (see Fig. 10.2A). Loud systolic murmurs radiate into the suprasternal notch and the base of the neck, especially the left side. Intensity varies directly with the degree of obstruction, but intensity per se is not necessarily an index of severity. In neonates with pinpoint pulmonary stenosis, the murmur is deceptively soft (see Fig. 10.1 lower A, B). Grade 3/6 murmurs are features of mild pulmonary stenosis (see Fig. 10.16), and grade 3/6 to 6/6 murmurs are features of moderate to severe pulmonary stenosis (see Figs. 10.17 through 10.19).

The severity determines the duration of right ventricular ejection that in turn determines the duration of the systolic murmur. However, the murmur of pinpoint pulmonary stenosis (see Fig. 10.1, lower) is disarmingly soft. Murmurs at nonprecordial thoracic sites accompany pulmonary artery stenosis and in neonates and infants are easily overlooked or lost in the rapid breath sounds.

The length of the murmur relative to the aortic component of the second heart sound permits comparison of the duration of right and left ventricular ejection (see Fig. 10.15). When pulmonary stenosis is mild, right ventricle remains normal, so a symmetric systolic murmur ends before the aortic component of the second sound (see Figs. 10.15 and 10.16).86 When stenosis is moderate, the murmur ends at or slightly after the aortic component of the second sound which remains audible (see Figs. 10.15 and 10.17).86 When stenosis is severe, the murmur extends beyond the aortic component which is partially or completely obscured (see Figs. 10.15, 10.18, and 10.19).86 With a still greater increase in severity, the murmur lengthens further, peaks later in systole, and assumes an asymmetric kite-shape.85,86 Fig. 10.15 illustrates the relationship between the duration and configuration of the systolic murmur and the degree of pulmonary stenosis. Stenosis of the ostium of the infundibulum (see Figs. 10.6 and 10.7) is accompanied by a murmur that is maximal in the third and fourth left intercostal spaces (see Fig. 10.19).13,86 Subinfundibular stenosis assigns the murmur still lower—to the fourth or fifth left intercostal space.87

Several types of diastolic murmurs occur, although rarely, in pulmonary valve stenosis. A low-intensity atrial systolic murmur is attributed to presystolic flow across the pulmonary valve (Fig. 10.20A).80 Powerful right atrial contraction generates a giant A wave that exceeds the diastolic pressure in the pulmonary trunk, so the pulmonary valve opens before the onset of ventricular contraction, permitting presystolic flow and a presystolic murmur (see Fig. 10.5).78,80,86 Presystolic murmurs are occasionally generated by prolonged vibrations of a fourth heart sound,78 and soft diastolic murmurs have been attributed to low-pressure pulmonary regurgitation (see Figs. 10.2B, 10.5, and 10.20B).80,86 Dysplastic or calcific pulmonary valves88 are rarely incompetent.

Systolic murmurs of pulmonary artery stenosis are crescendodecrescendo (see Figs. 10.21 and 10.22) with delayed onset because of their relatively distal origins (see Fig. 10.22). When the intensities of precordial and nonprecordial murmurs are equal, it can be assumed that the widespread nonprecordial murmurs originate peripherally. Intrapulmonary phonocardiograms confirm that systolic murmurs originate distal to stenoses in the pulmonary trunk and proximal pulmonary arterial branches (see Figs. 10.21 through 10.23) Peripheral pulmonary systolic murmurs are overlooked because of their low intensity and because auscultation is not routinely conducted at nonprecordial sites. The difficulty is compounded in infants because of rapid respiratory rates and because the frequency composition of breath sounds is close to the frequency of composition of peripheral pulmonary systolic murmurs. The diaphragm of the stethoscope should be applied during held respiration with the patient supine, prone, and sitting comfortably.
